items.summary: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.
items.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation

items.summary: Large language model agents increasingly use third-party tools to complete user tasks. Even without malicious intent, they may fill broad or weakly constrained fields with private information that is unnecessary or inappropriate for the receiving tool. Such calls can satisfy the tool schema and complete the task, yet still violate minimum-necessary disclosure. We introduce ArguShield, a mediation layer that intercepts proposed tool calls before execution. It evaluates each candidate value using three signals: Value Provenance, Task Relevance, and Disclosure Boundary. ArguShield releases justified values, defers values that need user confirmation, and withholds those outside the permitted scope. We evaluate ArguShield with four tool-calling models on ArgPrivBench, a benchmark of 120 tasks across Travel, Shopping, and Healthcare. items.summary: Differentially private zeroth-order optimization (DPZO) is a promising approach for privacy-preserving LLM fine-tuning, offering exceptional memory efficiency. However, its utility is highly sensitive to the clipping threshold $C$, a key DP-specific hyperparameter that controls the trade-off between noise injection and clipping bias. Existing DPZO methods typically tune $C$ by repeatedly evaluating candidate values and reporting the best result, which is computationally expensive and incurs additional privacy cost that must be accounted for under DP. Designing a practical DP procedure for selecting $C$ in DPZO is challenging because no fixed choice performs well across settings, straightforward search-based strategies suffer from poor utility and efficiency, and existing clipping-selection methods for DPSGD do not transfer well to DPZO due to its fundamentally different error regime. In this paper, we propose AutoClip-DPZO, a practical DP method that automatically and efficiently selects $C$ for DPZO. Our key idea is to avoid fine-tuning-based search by reducing clipping selection to a private quantile estimation problem, where the target quantile depends only on public privacy and training parameters. To derive this selection rule, we develop a novel characterization of DPZO error as a function of $C$ that captures both noise variance and clipping bias while remaining accurate and easy to optimize. Experiments show that AutoClip-DPZO achieves utility comparable to that obtained with the optimal $C$, while avoiding repeated fine-tuning-based search and incurring negligible additional overhead. Moreover, AutoClip-DPZO does not rely on sensitive hyperparameters.

items.summary: Security benchmarks for LLM agents record whether each attack succeeded and compare agents, attacks, and defenses by attack success rate (ASR). Such comparisons are valid only if the agent, the attack, and the defense cause each verdict. We show that verdicts also depend on content-free state: details of a run that carry no information about the system under test, such as the Python hash seed, the order of tools or evidence, and the scoring of failed runs. We require that this state influence no verdict (decision noninterference) and treat it as untrusted input, because evaluators and requesters of LLM-based gates can choose it. Our framework, TARE (Testing Attribution of Reported Effects), attributes a reported effect to the agent, attack, or defense only if it exceeds the measured influence of content-free state. On Agent Security Bench (ASB), runs with a fixed hash seed are identical for seven agents from four model families, yet changing the seed changes up to 17% of an agent's verdicts while the ASR moves by at most 5 points. The seed acts through the tool order: sorting the tool list instead of reverse-sorting it raises the ASR by up to 19 points, because ASB's naming convention places attacker tools first. When the same evidence is reordered, six of seven LLM judges change their decision on 17-91% of 98 proposed actions. Across eighteen agent-defense combinations, TARE's worst-case test attributes effects to two of three defenses, one of them in opposite directions on two agents, and a test fixed in advance confirms a 4.8-point decrease from the third; in the attributed decreases, 35-69% of the stopped attacks end without any tool call, which ASB counts as a failed attack. Reproducible verdicts are thus not necessarily attributable, and security evaluations of LLM agents should report the influence of content-free state. We release TARE, the ASB patch, and all verdict tables.

items.summary: Relative security (RS) judges a system against a reference system, but has only been applied to confidentiality. We introduce relative integrity (RI), which states that every behaviour a system exhibits under an attacker's influence must be one the reference can exhibit for the same trusted inputs. RS and RI each choose their own reference runs, so together they accept attacks whose leak and effects the reference reproduces only in different runs. We therefore develop a further property, relative robustness (RR), which asks the same runs to reproduce both and is strictly stronger than RS and RI together. We give proof methods for RI and RR and a disproof method for RI, and apply them in two domains: (1) LLM agents under prompt injection, where the reference runs the same plan with a model that never obeys untrusted content, and (2) C programs partitioned across an SGX or TrustZone enclave boundary, where the reference keeps every function inside. We evaluate the properties on models of five published attacks, a support desk, an OP-TEE HOTP token and common agent defences. Two cases pass RS and RI but fail RR: an injection that makes the support desk's model accept any customer, as one input did in the Tensor Trust game, and the simulation step of the attack on Secret Network, in which an SGX enclave reveals a transfer's outcome without committing it. Our work is fully mechanised in Isabelle/HOL, with the enclave programs verified in C using AutoCorres2.

items.summary: LLM coding agents authorize shell commands by parsing a command string against a policy and passing the raw string to a system shell, so the gate adjudicates one reading while the shell executes another. We present ParseGap, a differential testing framework that runs each command through an unmodified vendor checker and GNU Bash 5.2 in an isolated container, flagging a violation whenever an approved command produces policy-violating runtime effects. Live trials across two frontier models triggered policy violations in all 16 agent-model pairs (14 under configured restrictions). To eliminate the second reading, we design ShellPlan, which compiles a strict Bash subset once into a typed execution plan, validates utility arguments against positive capability specifications, and dispatches approved plans directly via execve without a shell. Over a formal operational model, we prove single-interpretation dispatch and bound touched programs and files under audited assumptions. ShellPlan admitted 0/4,174 active attacks across six static suites and 0/90 hits in a ten-model agent benchmark (62/90 unguarded) at 1.28 ms median gate latency, preserving 36/36 (100%) frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall) and 0/348 external over-allows outside modeled exceptions.

items.summary: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.

items.summary: In near-field physical-layer authentication (PLA), the receiver estimates a spatial reference from noisy enrollment pilots. With a fixed residual-energy threshold, even a small reference error can cause the false rejection (FR) probability to approach one as the received energy increases. We derive the distribution of the overlap between the true and enrolled spatial directions and use it to calibrate a test based on the aligned energy and the residual-to-aligned energy ratio. The calibration bounds FR for arbitrary regional gains and all legitimate received energies above a prescribed minimum. For a fixed enrolled reference, we reduce the problem of finding the maximum acceptance probability of a multi-antenna attacker to a one-dimensional search. We also derive a pre-enrollment upper bound that holds when the attacker chooses its precoder after observing the enrolled reference. For a single region and a fixed angular threshold, the enrollment energy sufficient to preserve angular separation grows inversely with the square of the available angular margin. In the numerical study with 128 receive elements at 28 GHz, the FR upper bound was 0.9984, including the enrollment outage allowance. At a regional phase perturbation of 20, four regions provided the best trade-off among the tested partitions: its simulated FR was 0.1442, while its false acceptance (FA) at 9 m was 1.084 under the fixed transmit-energy setting.

items.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

items.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.

items.summary: AI coding agents now triage issues, review pull requests and pick up tasks inside GitHub repositories, and to do so they read text that anyone with a GitHub account can write. This makes GitHub a prime surface for indirect prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in untrusted content steer a model that later processes it. Prior work has demonstrated such attacks against agents on GitHub in controlled settings, but how often they occur in practice, who deploys them, and for what purpose remain unknown. We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI-directed hidden text on GitHub. We analyzed roughly 145 million issues, pull requests, comments and README files, detected text that GitHub does not render to a human reader but that an agent receives in full, and filtered it with a two-stage LLM classification, a template provenance check and an exhaustive manual review. We identify 2,281 validated findings in issues, pull requests and comments (16 per million items), and AI-directed hidden text in the READMEs of 107 repositories. We find a heterogeneous ecosystem of four uses: attacks on other parties' agents, defensive text that restricts agents, content override that steers what they write, and first-party orchestration, in which projects coordinate their own agents through hidden markers. Attacks are rare (about one in 3.3 million items) but aimed at maintainers' own triage, review and CI agents. Orchestration accounts for two thirds of the findings in issues, pull requests and comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel that anyone who can comment can imitate. Replayed offline against five models we tested, the attacks succeed against one small, fast model in 19% of cases, and against none once HTML comments are stripped. We release our detection tool and every finding.

For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

items.summary: Open-weight language models are vulnerable to trigger-conditioned behaviors introduced through sparse post-training weight modifications, creating supply-chain risks beyond conventional provenance checks. We present Neural Sentinel, a cross-architecture study of gradient-guided backdoor insertion and model forensics spanning 18 checkpoints across 14 architecture families (124M-31.3B parameters), including state-space and recurrent models. On Phi-2, modifying approximately 0.0002% of parameters induced an exact short-marker output after 300 steps (332 seconds), with mean next-token KL divergence of $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ and 100% top-1 agreement over evaluated positions of eight fixed reference prompts. Separate experiments produced structured tool-call-formatted outputs without establishing downstream execution. We identify three procedure-dependent response regimes -- Gradient-Permeable, Scale-Threshold, and Gradient-Fragmented -- and evaluate PPO-based weight-space exploration, which showed no statistically significant advantage over random search. For defense, Neural Sentinel combines weight-difference analysis, trigger discovery, activation probing, and contextual output inspection. In a 22-artifact development cohort, its reference-optional scanner classified 4/5 backdoored artifacts as BACKDOORED; the remaining positive and all 17 clean artifacts were SUSPICIOUS. These findings establish the feasibility of sparse conditional-output insertion and evidence-producing forensic triage, while identifying limitations in behavioral-drift assessment and clean-model admission.

items.summary: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.
items.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration

items.summary: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.
items.title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection

items.summary: @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web framework. In versions 4.0.7 through 4.0.9, the plugin does not rewrite regular-expression mount paths to account for a parameterized plugin prefix, so when middleware is mounted with a regular expression inside a plugin registered under a parameterized prefix, the Express matcher treats the prefix parameter as literal text and never matches the real request path. As a result, Express silently skips that middleware while Fastify still runs the route handler, so an application that relies on regular-expression mounted middleware for authentication or authorization inside a parameterized-prefix plugin exposes protected routes to unauthenticated clients. No special configuration is required beyond a parameterized prefix and a regular-expression mount. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.10, and users should upgrade to 4.0.10 or later.

items.summary: The Restrictions for BuddyPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution in all versions up to, and including, 1.5.4 This is due to the plugin splicing the attacker-controlled request URI into a PHP expression inside a double-quoted string and evaluating it with eval(). Because PHP interpolates double-quoted strings, a payload of the form {${...}} in the URL path is executed during interpolation, so no quote breakout is required and WordPress' slashing does not mitigate it. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server with a single GET request. The affected conditions ship enabled by default and are evaluated before any logged-in check, so no plugin configuration is needed; the site must have BuddyPress and Paid Memberships Pro active alongside this plugin.

items.summary: The Nexter Blocks Pro plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 5.0.10 via the `tpgb_ajax_register_user()` function. This is due to a byte-level denylist on the `tpgb_acf_key[]` and `tpgb_acf[]` parameters that fails to block Unicode look-alike characters — such as U+1E87 and U+00E7 in a key like `ẇp_çapabilities` — whose UTF-8 byte sequences do not match any ASCII-based pattern check, while the database's default accent-insensitive collation (`utf8mb4_unicode_ci` / `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`) treats the decorated key as equivalent to the canonical `wp_capabilities` row, causing `update_user_meta()` to overwrite the newly registered user's role with `administrator`. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to register a new account bearing the full Administrator role, gaining complete control over the WordPress site including the ability to install plugins, modify files, and execute arbitrary code. The nonce required by the handler is publicly emitted on any page containing the tp-login-register block, making the full exploit chain — nonce retrieval, a single crafted registration POST, and the plugin's own `autologin` flow — trivially reachable on any default install where user registration is enabled. Successful exploitation causes the attacker's own account to receive the complete Administrator role.

items.summary:
XML::Sig versions before 0.74 for Perl allow code execution via a document's Algorithm attribute that verify resolves to a function name and calls.

The text after the last `#` in the DigestMethod and SignatureMethod Algorithm attributes is looked up with Digest::SHA->can. That returns a code reference for any fully qualified function name, Perl builtins in the CORE namespace included. The digest function is called on the canonical form of the referenced element, so the document picks both the function and its argument.

An attacker who can submit a signed document can run a command as the verifying process.

items.summary:
Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences vulnerability in ufirstgroup ymlr (Ymlr module) allows attackers to inject arbitrary content into generated YAML documents through document comments. Ymlr.document!/2 interpolates each caller-supplied comment string into the output behind a single # prefix without validating it or escaping line breaks. Because a YAML comment is terminated by a line break, the first carriage return or line feed in the comment string ends the comment context and everything after it is emitted at column 0 of the document body.

An attacker who controls text that the host application passes as a comment can forge top-level mapping keys, override values the application itself set, and emit --- or ... markers that split the output into additional documents. Downstream consumers of the generated YAML, such as configuration loaders, deployment manifests, CI pipelines and data importers, parse the injected content as legitimate data. The same clause backs Ymlr.document/2, Ymlr.documents!/2 and Ymlr.documents/2, so every document encoding entry point is affected.

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ymlr.ex and program routines Ymlr.document!/2, Ymlr.documents!/2.

This issue affects ymlr: from 0.0.1 before 5.1.6.

items.summary:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ninenines cowboy allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust connection process memory over HTTP/1.1.

The HTTP/1.1 handler in cowboy_http enforces the max_headers limit by counting the number of distinct header names in a map (maps:size(Headers)). When a request contains multiple header lines with the same name, the values are concatenated into a single ever-growing binary stored under that one map key (", " for regular headers, "; " for cookies), so the map size stays at one and the max_headers cap (default 100) is never reached. Because no accumulator bounds the total number of header lines or the total byte size of the header block (only per-line max_header_name_length and max_header_value_length apply), an unauthenticated client can send an arbitrary number of header lines with the same name and grow the connection process's binary memory to arbitrary size within the request window.

The impact per connection is bounded by request_timeout (default 5 seconds, not reset by header data), and by max_heap_size when set (the offending connection process is killed once its heap grows past the limit). When max_heap_size is left at the default (unset), sustained abuse can drive the Erlang VM into out-of-memory conditions.

This issue affects cowboy: from 2.0.0-pre.4 before 2.18.0.

items.summary:
Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in mtrudel bandit allows unauthenticated remote denial of service via CPU exhaustion during WebSocket fragment reassembly.

The size guard Bandit.WebSocket.Connection.oversize_message?/2 called from handle_frame/3 in lib/bandit/websocket/connection.ex appends each non-final continuation frame to a left-nested iolist and then re-measures the entire accumulated buffer with IO.iodata_length/1 on every frame. Because the buffer grows by one element per frame and is fully re-traversed each time, reassembly work is quadratic (O(n^2)) in the number of continuation frames.

The max_fragmented_message_size limit (default 8 MB) bounds total bytes but not frame count, and each frame can carry as little as one payload byte, so an attacker can send millions of tiny continuation frames using modest bandwidth to pin a CPU core for minutes to hours. Many concurrent connections can starve the whole server of CPU, denying service to legitimate users. The WebSocket read timeout does not help, because it is an idle timeout evaluated between reads and cannot preempt the synchronous reassembly work spent inside a single callback.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.11.0 before 1.12.1.

items.summary:
Allocation of resources without limits vulnerability in ninenines cowlib allows an unauthenticated remote HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 peer to exhaust memory on the vulnerable server (or client) and cause a denial of service.

The HPACK and QPACK prefixed-integer decoder cow_hpack_common:dec_big_int/3 in src/cow_hpack_common.hrl (invoked from cow_hpack:decode/2 in src/cow_hpack.erl and from cow_qpack:decode_field_section/3 in src/cow_qpack.erl) reads continuation octets until it sees one whose high bit is clear, evaluating Int + (Value bsl M) at each step with the shift M growing by seven per octet. No limit is enforced on the number of continuation octets, on the resulting bit width, or on the value; the decoder consumes whatever encoded length the peer supplies.

Because Erlang integers are immutable, each intermediate Value bsl M and each accumulator update allocates a fresh bignum whose digit width grows linearly with the number of octets processed so far. Summed across the whole decode, the transient bignum digit materialization is on the order of the square of the encoded length. A single maximal HPACK indexed representation carried inside one HTTP/2 HEADERS plus one CONTINUATION frame at Cowboy's default max_frame_size_received can force hundreds of megabytes of transient allocation and garbage-collection churn before the resulting header-table index is rejected as invalid. Repeated or concurrent connections multiply the pressure and can drive the Erlang VM to memory exhaustion.

Cowlib is the HTTP parser used by Cowboy, RabbitMQ's management plugin, and other Erlang and Elixir HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 servers and clients, so any exposed endpoint that accepts HPACK or QPACK from an untrusted peer is reachable.

This issue affects cowlib: from 2.0.0-pre.1 before 2.19.0.

items.summary:
Allocation of resources without limits vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a remote HTTP/2 server to exhaust memory on the client host and cause a denial of service.

The Mint.HTTP2.handle_continuation/3 function in lib/mint/http2.ex accumulates the header-block fragment carried by each HTTP/2 CONTINUATION frame into a growing conn.headers_being_processed nesting, one level deeper per frame, and only releases it when a frame with the END_HEADERS flag arrives. The only guard on this accumulator is Mint.HTTP2.assert_header_block_within_max_size/2, which sums the byte size of the fragments received so far. Because a CONTINUATION frame is permitted by the protocol to carry a zero-length payload, an unbounded chain of zero-length CONTINUATION frames adds no bytes to the running total, never trips the size cap, and never emits END_HEADERS, yet each frame still nests the accumulator one level deeper.

A malicious HTTP/2 server (reachable directly, via an attacker-controlled redirect, via SSRF, or via a man-in-the-middle) can open a stream by sending a HEADERS frame without END_HEADERS and then stream zero-length CONTINUATION frames indefinitely. Client memory grows one cons cell per frame received; sustained bandwidth from the peer drives the BEAM node running the Mint client to memory exhaustion and eventual out-of-memory termination.

This issue affects mint: from 0.1.0 before 1.9.2.

Plug.Parsers.MULTIPART, the multipart request-body parser used to handle file uploads and multipart forms, does not enforce its :length budget against all consumed resources, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause denial of service. items.summary:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in elixir-mint mint (Mint.HTTP1 module) allows a denial of service via an oversized chunked transfer-encoded response.

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/mint/http1.ex and program routines Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5, Mint.HTTP1.add_body_to_buffer/2.

When Mint decodes a chunked HTTP response body, it accumulates each partial fragment of the current chunk in the connection's data_buffer (an unbounded iolist) via add_body_to_buffer/2 and does not emit the data to the caller until the full declared chunk length has been received. The chunk size is taken directly from the server and parsed with no upper bound, so a malicious or compromised server can announce one enormous chunk (for example a size line of 7FFFFFFF, about 2 GiB) and then send the body bytes slowly without ever completing the chunk. The client buffers every received byte while it waits for a completion that never arrives, and because no data responses are produced until the chunk finishes, a caller that otherwise streams large content-length bodies safely gains no protection. An unauthenticated remote server (reachable whenever a client follows redirects, fetches user-supplied URLs, or processes webhooks) can drive the client's memory arbitrarily high and trigger an out-of-memory condition.

This issue affects mint: from 0.5.0 before 1.9.1.

items.summary:
Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes vulnerability in ash-project ash allows a user to set the value of a private action argument that is intended to be controlled only by trusted server-side code.

Action arguments declared with public?: false are meant to be set internally (for example via Ash.Changeset.set_private_argument/3) and must not be settable from end-user input. When a changeset is built from a parameter map, Ash filters out private arguments, but the filtering is incomplete.

In the regular changeset path (for_create, for_update, for_destroy), private arguments are stripped only when the parameter key is an atom. When the key is a binary (string), as is the case for user-supplied parameters, the private argument is kept and the user controls its value. In the atomic path (Ash.Changeset.fully_atomic_changeset/4, also reached through atomic and bulk updates), private arguments are not stripped at all, regardless of whether the key is an atom or a binary.

An attacker who can submit parameters to an action that defines a private argument can therefore inject a value for that argument. Depending on how the application uses the argument (for example an acting_user_id driving authorization or record ownership), this can lead to an integrity violation or privilege escalation.

This issue affects ash: from 3.0.0-rc.0 before 3.29.3.

items.summary:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in ueberauth guardian (Guardian.Permissions module) allows a denial of service via BEAM atom-table exhaustion.

This vulnerability is associated with program file lib/guardian/permissions.ex and program routines Guardian.Permissions.encode_permissions!/1, Guardian.Permissions.encode_permissions_into_claims!/2, Guardian.Permissions.do_encode_permissions!/2.

The Guardian.Permissions mixin installs a public encode_permissions!/1 function on every module that does use Guardian.Permissions. For each key of the supplied map, encode_permissions!/1 calls String.to_atom(to_string(k)) before any validation runs. The integer-value clause of do_encode_permissions!/2 then short-circuits straight to encoding without validating the key against the configured permission set, so a key with an integer value is interned as a fresh atom with no exception raised. Atoms are never garbage collected and the BEAM atom table is a fixed-size resource (default roughly 1,048,576 entries), so each unique attacker-chosen key permanently consumes one slot. An attacker who can influence a permission map that reaches encode_permissions!/1 (for example a permissions map read from a request body and passed into token issuance via encode_permissions_into_claims!/2) can mint an unbounded number of atoms and exhaust the atom table, crashing the entire BEAM node and every service running on it. The sibling decode_permissions/1 is not affected because it skips keys absent from the configured permission set.

This issue affects guardian: from 1.0.0-beta.0 before 2.4.1.

items.summary:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling in ueberauth guardian allows denial of service via unbounded atom creation from attacker-controlled binary input.

Guardian.Permissions.AtomEncoding encodes permission scopes by passing arbitrary binaries to String.to_atom/1. When encode/3 in lib/guardian/permissions/atom_encoding.ex is called with a list, each binary entry is handled by the encode_value/3 binary clause, which calls String.to_atom(value) with no allow-list check. The perm_set argument (the application's small, finite set of legitimate permission names) is discarded, so any external string flows straight into atom creation. This encoder is selected with use Guardian.Permissions, encoding: Guardian.Permissions.AtomEncoding and reached through the imported encode/3 entry point.

String.to_atom/1 creates a brand-new atom for every previously unseen binary, atoms are never garbage collected, and the BEAM atom table is fixed at roughly 1,048,576 entries by default. An application that funnels attacker-influenced permission scopes (from a request body, a JWT claim, or other external input) into encode/3 therefore mints one permanent atom per distinct value. A modest stream of varied, unauthenticated input permanently consumes the atom table and crashes the BEAM node with system_limit, taking down every application running on it.

The default encoder is Guardian.Permissions.BitwiseEncoding, which is not affected.

This issue affects guardian: from 2.0.0 before 2.4.1.

An attacker who controls the Markdown text can supply a javascript: URL (for example [click](javascript:alert(document.cookie))) that survives verbatim into the Delta attribute. When the Delta is rendered to HTML by a downstream renderer (such as quill-delta-to-html or the Quill client), the attribute becomes an or , and the javascript: scheme executes in the browser of anyone who views the rendered content. The link and wikilink cases are the strongest vectors because javascript: in an href executes on click; the image case is lower impact because javascript: in generally does not execute in modern browsers. This issue affects mdex: from 0.8.3 before 0.13.2.

items.summary:
Uncontrolled Recursion vulnerability in leandrocp mdex allows denial of service via deeply nested Markdown input.

mdex converts between an Elixir %MDEx.Document{} struct and Comrak's internal AST using two mutually recursive Rust functions, ex_document_to_comrak_ast and comrak_ast_to_ex_document, in the NIF source file document.rs. Neither function enforces a maximum nesting depth, so the recursion depth is bounded only by the structure of the input. An attacker who can get a Markdown document rendered (for example through MDEx.parse_document!/1 or MDEx.to_html/1) can supply a document with thousands of nested block quotes, which drives unbounded recursion across the NIF boundary and exhausts the native C stack.

Because the resulting stack overflow is an uncatchable SIGSEGV raised inside a NIF, it cannot be contained by the Erlang runtime. It terminates the operating system process running the BEAM, killing every Elixir and Erlang process on the node, not just the caller that triggered the render. No authentication or special privileges are required.

The vulnerable conversion code was extracted from mdex into the separate mdex_native package starting in mdex 0.12.3.

This issue affects mdex: from 0.3.0 before 0.12.3; mdex_native: from 0.1.0 before 0.2.3.

items.summary:
Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability in malach-it Boruta allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause the OAuth/OpenID authorization server to issue outbound HTTP requests to attacker-chosen URIs, including internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.

Three code paths fetch remote URIs supplied by the requester without sufficient validation of the target. Boruta.Oauth.Request.Base.fetch_unsigned_request/1 in lib/boruta/oauth/request/base.ex dereferences the OAuth request_uri parameter from the authorization request via Finch.build(:get, request_uri) |> Finch.request(OpenIDHttpClient). Boruta.Openid.parse_registration_params/2 in lib/boruta/openid.ex dereferences the jwks_uri supplied in an OpenID Connect dynamic client registration request. Boruta.Ecto.Clients.refresh_jwk_from_jwks_uri/1 in lib/boruta/adapters/ecto/clients.ex later refreshes the stored jwks_uri for an existing client. In all three paths the only validation is that the URI parses with a scheme (and one of the two request_uri clauses does not even restrict the scheme to http or https). The implementations do not require HTTPS, do not enforce a host or IP allowlist, do not reject loopback, private, link-local, or other non-public ranges after DNS resolution, do not cap response size, and do not constrain redirects. An attacker can therefore steer the server's HTTP client at arbitrary network targets reachable from the Boruta host.

This issue affects boruta: from 2.3.2 before 2.3.7 and from 3.0.0-beta.1 onward.

From 0.11.0 until 0.11.4, add_subscription() in amqtt/broker.py accepts malformed single-level + wildcard placement because it checks substrings instead of validating each slash-delimited level. The _matches() function converts each + into a greedy regular-expression fragment and evaluates it with re.fullmatch(), allowing a filter containing many adjacent + characters to trigger catastrophic backtracking when compared with a topic that partially matches but ultimately fails. Because matching runs synchronously in _run_broadcast(), one subscription followed by a publish can block the broker event loop, stopping message delivery and new connection processing until restart. Anonymous clients can trigger the issue with the default configuration. Any authenticated client permitted to create arbitrary subscriptions and publish messages may still exploit it when authentication is enabled. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.4.

Selecting a personal folder as the new parent passed the personal-folder guard and set personal_folder on the target, transferring the credential subtree into the attacker's accessible space after the next login and hiding it from the organization, including administrators. The change exposed credential labels, logins, URLs, email addresses, and descriptions, while sharekey-protected passwords remained protected; hiding the subtree also denied other users access. This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.2.

Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code or inject SQL through a forged keyset pagination cursor.

Ash.Page.Keyset.filter/4 in lib/ash/page/keyset.ex decodes the client-supplied page[:after] or page[:before] cursor from Erlang external term format and rejects decoded expressions with Ash.Expr.expr?/1. A struct in the cursor value for such a sort field therefore reaches the data layer. With AshPostgres, the read passes such a struct to inspect/1, which runs the Inspect implementation of the struct module that the attacker selected. A chain of struct modules from ecto and db_connection then calls a function that the cursor names, which permits OS command execution. An %Ash.Query.Function.Fragment{} inside an %Ash.CiString{} value is written into the SQL query as raw text.

This issue affects ash: from 3.31.3 before 3.38.0.

items.summary: RabbitMQ is a messaging and streaming broker. In the affected revision identified by the advisory, the AMQP 1.0 server_mode parser in deps/amqp10_common/src/amqp10_binary_parser.erl stops at the first body section and preserves the remaining bytes in bare_and_footer without validating message-section order. An authenticated publisher with write permission can place a properties section carrying a forged user-id after the body, causing rabbit_access_control:check_user_id/2 to see no user-id while permissive downstream AMQP 1.0 decoders or AMQP 0-9-1 conversion through classic and quorum queues expose the forged identity. Applications that rely on RabbitMQ-validated user-id metadata can therefore accept attacker-controlled publisher attribution. Strict consumers that reject out-of-order sections are not vulnerable to identity spoofing, and the issue does not bypass broker routing or destination authorization. items.summary: Lookyloo is a web-based URL capture and analysis platform. Prior to the fix, the authorization mechanism for private captures (seed-based access control) was not consistently enforced at the data access layer. The capture_cache method and numerous internal methods (get_info, get_meta, get_statistics, get_modules_responses, get_data, get_video, get_screenshot, get_har, get_cookies, get_storage_state, get_frames, get_console_messages, get_capture, get_ressource, misp_export, lacus_export, ai_export, comparator functions, and others) could be invoked with only a capture UUID without validating the required seed token. This meant that API endpoints and internal code paths that called these methods directly could return private capture data to unauthenticated users or users lacking the correct seed. The before_request hook in the web interface provided a partial check, but the underlying data layer did not enforce it, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary. An attacker who knew or guessed a private capture UUID could potentially access sensitive data including rendered screenshots, HAR files, downloaded files, cookies, storage state, console messages, and MISP exports through various REST API endpoints and web routes. The fix introduces a LookylooPrivateCapture exception raised at the cache layer when a private capture is accessed without a valid seed, refactors the API to pass CaptureCache objects (already validated) rather than raw UUIDs, and ensures all web and API endpoints propagate the session-known seed or admin status to the data access layer. Background processes use an explicit unsafe=True flag to bypass the check, as they operate server-side with full trust.

items.summary: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, when the pipelined request queue is full, the pure-Python parser stores the unparsed remainder internally and also returns the same data to its caller. After a handler declines an upgrade request, the caller feeds the remainder back to the parser, causing the buffer to grow with each handled request and dispatching already-handled requests to the application again. The issue affects deployments using AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS or otherwise running without the standard C-extension wheel, and can cause excessive memory use and repeated request processing. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

Prior to 3.14.4, aiohttp decompresses each member of a payload containing many concatenated gzip, deflate, or zstd streams by passing the entire remaining input to a new decompressor, causing quadratic CPU use. Empty members produce no output, so client_max_size and output backpressure do not limit the work. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

items.summary: We study message authentication over a public channel against a computationally unbounded adversary. Motivated by low-complexity applications, we consider schemes that leverage off-the-shelf binary linear codes already used for error correction in communication systems. Existing code-based constructions derive an authentication tag primarily from a single symbol in a $q$-ary code, which limits the tag length. However, selecting several binary coordinates allows a fixed binary linear code to support different tag lengths. We characterize how coordinate selection and ordering affect the statistical guarantees against impersonation and substitution attacks. In particular, we explore three methods: the subset selector, the ordered selector, and the independent selector. They read uniformly chosen coordinates in a fixed public or a secret random order, or with replacement, and add a uniform mask. With a fresh key per message, all three achieve the optimal impersonation probability $2^{-l_t}$ for $l_t$-bit tags. We bound the subset selector's substitution probability using only nonzero weights. Those of the other two depend only on the code length $n$, $l_t$, and the nonzero weight farthest from $n/2$. The independent selector achieves $2^{-l_t}$ for substitution when all nonzero weights equal $n/2$. Finally, we evaluate first-order Reed-Muller and Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem dual subcodes.
items.title: Code-Based Message Authentication with Statistical Guarantees via Coordinate Selection and Masking

items.summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

items.summary: An audit recorder must permit exact recovery with a small private index before it knows which questions a future reader will ask. A recursion on question partitions generates the decision trees, their eventwise costs and the price equations. A common-optimal-tree criterion explains when reduction to a fractional cover preserves the result. On uniform binary linear event spaces with four private roles, if every quartet is split evenly by some bit, optimal identification probability at expected follow-up budget $b$ is $(1+b)/2$. Otherwise it is $\min(1/2+b/3,3/4)$. We characterize all priors attaining the latter curve in its rising regime and derive a closed-form compiler for three binary fields. For a population tilted by one pairwise parity we obtain the full budget curve and a single recorder attaining it. On eight negotiated TLS suites the aligned populations allow a 60 percent follow-up rate at a 70 percent identification ceiling. A pairwise correlation with unchanged marginal field frequencies reduces that maximum to 40 percent. Across 960 local TLS sessions, the recorder recovered every negotiated suite using two private bits per session.
items.title: The Privacy Cost of Writing an Audit Receipt Before Its Context Is Known

items.summary: Modern commodity DPI systems are capable of analyzing packet sizes, directions, and timings to detect circumvention tools even when those tools use sophisticated obfuscation. The anti-censorship community has called for innovation in traffic shaping and built an ecosystem that facilitates the adoption of new shaping techniques. However, a fundamental gap is halting progress: \textit{what} should circumvention traffic look like? Past experience with traffic shaping has underscored that effective shaping must produce traffic that looks like legitimate Internet traffic while limiting the ability of censors to identify multiple proxies through shared fingerprints. In this paper, we use our access to large-scale real-world TLS traffic at a regional ISP to analyze approximately 12 million connections, finding that individual servers differ substantially from the broader TLS population and that traffic patterns vary across services. Combining these empirical observations with past experience with traffic shaping, we build CenShaper, which shapes each proxy's traffic to look like a selected TLS server. To reproduce these server-specific patterns, CenShaper trains a shared generative model using traffic from TLS connections to many servers and adapts it for each proxy using a small sample of recorded connections to its selected server. Our model evaluation shows that fingerprints learned from known proxies transfer poorly to proxies imitating previously unseen TLS services. In end-to-end testing, CenShaper reduces the detection rate of TLS-over-TLS fingerprinting from over 85\% to approximately 3\% at a 1\% false positive rate. Finally, we show how running CenShaper as a sidecar process simplifies integration with existing circumvention tools, making it a practical defense against increasingly powerful traffic analysis attacks.
items.title: CenShaper: Shaping Proxy Traffic for Censorship Circumvention

items.summary: Recent incidents involving agents bypassing sandboxing and network isolation have raised concerns about existing agent harnesses, prompting frontier labs such as OpenAI to reevaluate the security of their training platforms. Incident reviews show that determined agents can escape processes, containers, and VMs, or bypass their isolation through advanced side and covert channels. Follow-up audits also found that some agents concealed their actions by disabling monitoring and tampering with logs. We propose Airlock, an architecture that pairs each agent's VM with an Airlock VM, each running in a separate hardware-isolated Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). The Airlock VM fully mediates the agent's interactions with the outside world, including network and storage operations. We modify the firmware layer of Arm's Confidential Computing Architecture, Realm Management Monitor (RMM), and the kernels of both VMs so that the Airlock VM serves the agent VM's IO without involving the host. We adapt OpenShell, an agent runtime supporting sandboxing and governance policies, to this architecture. Airlock keeps network and filesystem policies, and credential protection effective even if the agent VM is fully compromised, and it removes the host from the agent's IO path, reducing opportunities for collusion and covert channels with the host. Finally, we extend the Airlock VM's capabilities to provide tamper-proof auditing of all agent operations, preserving forensic evidence even if the Airlock VM is compromised. We implement and evaluate Airlock on a Radxa development board. Our evaluation shows a loss of filesystem performance and network latency for small messages under 15% and a drop of network bandwidth by half or more, which in practice has a limited effect on typical agent tasks.
items.title: Airlock: Robust Sandboxing and Governance of Rogue Agents

items.summary: Agent Skills has gained widespread adoption as an open standard for extending agent capabilities. To facilitate skill sharing, public skill hubs have grown in popularity and increasingly rely on automated security detectors to identify malicious skills at scale. Yet, the effectiveness and limitations of these detectors remain insufficiently understood. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study of four hub-adopted and two community-provided malicious skill detectors on 1477 agent skills from seven datasets. Our evaluation reveals that even the best-performing hub-adopted detector by overall F1, skill-scanner with Qwen3.6, still misses 4.9% of malicious skills and incorrectly flags 17.8% of benign skills. To understand these failures, we manually analyze detectors' findings and decision-making processes, identifying two recurring failure mechanisms. False positives often arise when detectors flag sensitive operations, such as credential access, without considering whether they serve the skill's legitimate purpose. Conversely, false negatives occur when detectors recognize malicious instructions or behaviors but underestimate their severity or dismiss valid findings during review, ultimately leaving malicious skills unblocked. Guided by this analysis, we refine the prompts of a state-of-the-art detector, skill-vetter, improving its mean F1 score in eight of nine evaluation settings, with gains of up to 22.7 percentage points. These results highlight gaps in existing skill-vetting practices and underscore the need for more robust and context-aware detection mechanisms.
items.title: Demystifying Detectors Guarding Agent Skill Hubs

items.summary: Since 2023, bug bounty platforms have introduced participation rules, such as proof-of-concept mandates, against a flood of AI-generated low-quality submissions. The platforms set these rules, but vendors running programs on them bear the cost when a vulnerability goes unreported and gets exploited. We ask whether the rules benefit the vendors they are meant to protect. Adding to Gal-Or, Hydari, and Telang's 2024 model a vendor triage cost per report reviewed and a participation cost paid in effort by the researchers reporting vulnerabilities, we locate a threshold in an effective triage-burden parameter, which captures the vendor's processing burden per unit of aggregate search effort, with the rules lowering profit below it and raising it above. Because attackers never use the platform, the participation cost falls on researchers alone and fewer take part. Bug-finding coverage falls and breach damage rises, which costs the vendor, while its triage bill falls, which helps.
items.title: Bug Bounty Programs in the AI Era: How Does Platform Anti-Spam Friction Affect Vendor Profitability?

items.summary: While frontier language models are becoming capable cybersecurity assistants, they also create a dual-use cyber risk: the same capabilities that help defenders identify and analyze vulnerabilities can similarly help attackers weaponize them. Existing cyber benchmarks measure either raw offensive capability or generic refusal behavior, overlooking the dual-use cyber assessment of preserving benign security utility while refusing assistance that materially advances misuse. We introduce CyberDualEval, a benchmark with 430 vulnerable tasks for measuring dual-use cyber risk in frontier language models. Each task is decomposed into three phases of increasing operationalization: security analysis, proof-of-concept generation, and exploit generation. To quantify the residual cyber risk, we annotate each task with a Task Weaponization Score that measures how much work remains to turn the resulting artifact into unauthorized cyber misuse. CyberDualEval assesses ten closed- and open-weight language models both on correct compliance and on task performance, developing four deterministic mechanisms for determining per-phase success on a large subset of the dataset. Our evaluation reveals that none of the existing frontier models effectively navigate helping with safe requests and refusing risky ones, characterized by being overly-cautious. On the other hand, recent open-weight models rarely refuse and demonstrate strong validated accuracy on risky requests.
items.title: CyberDualEval: Measuring Dual-Use Cyber Risks in Frontier Language Models

items.summary: Remote timing attacks exploit variations in response times to infer sensitive information about remote systems. Their effectiveness, however, is often limited by the difficulty of accurately modeling the stochastic nature of server-side response times, taking into account the intrinsic variability of the service time of a request and the impact of varying workloads on the observed response times. In this article, we propose a new stochastic framework for remote timing attacks based on queuing models and Bayesian statistics. We assume that the attacker knows the service time distributions of two classes of requests and that the information leakage occurs when a malicious observer can distinguish with high probability the class based on the observed response times in the presence of noise induced by exogenous workload. Our experimental evaluation on popular websites demonstrates the practical viability of the approach: our attack outperforms formal techniques based on deterministic service times and existing empirical techniques, while requiring less tuning and fewer hyper-parameters compared to previous formal approaches. Overall, our results show that principled stochastic modeling can provide a solid foundation for building more effective remote timing attacks under realistic network and workload conditions.
items.title: Queuing for Secrets: Model-Based Remote Timing Attacks

items.summary: A central challenge in Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is the selection of ciphertext moduli, which depends on accurately estimating noise growth during homomorphic evaluation. Choosing excessively large moduli reduces the efficiency and scalability of the scheme, whereas underestimating noise can result in decryption failures and potential security vulnerabilities. Average-case analyses have provided promising probabilistic estimates of noise growth in practical FHE computations. However, recent studies indicate that reliable estimates must account for dependencies among ciphertext errors, as neglecting these correlations can systematically underestimate noise. This work presents the first average-case analysis for the BGV scheme that accounts for both correlations induced by secret/public keys and ciphertext dependencies. We propose new variance estimates for the noise coefficients in homomorphic additions and multiplications involving dependent ciphertexts, and extend our framework to the homomorphic evaluation of polynomial functions, which is widely employed in FHE applications. Our theoretical estimates closely align with experimental observations, exhibiting discrepancies smaller than 1.2 bits. Finally, these estimates are adopted to choose the initial BGV parameters, leading to significantly smaller ciphertext moduli compared to those currently adopted in widely used FHE libraries, thus improving the efficiency of the scheme. Compared to OpenFHE, we obtain an average reduction of about 11.5% in the ciphertext modulus size, while relative to HElib, we reduce the ratio between consecutive moduli up to 23 bits per level in practical settings.
items.title: From Dependent Ciphertexts to Sharp Bounds for Polynomial Evaluation in BGV

items.summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.
items.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?

items.summary: Mirror-based LiDAR attacks passively redirect automotive LiDAR's beams to create phantom objects in the vehicle perception. Recent work has demonstrated that these attacks may cause vehicles to brake for a phantom where nothing stands. Every phantom return is a genuine time-of-flight measurement, so current spoofing defenses are not able to differentiate phantoms from real objects. We present MirrorGuard, a physics-informed defense that identifies and removes mirror-induced phantom returns before they affect downstream perception. MirrorGuard tests three consequences of the reflected path. Every phantom bearing crosses the mirror's finite aperture, its opaque surface blocks any direct return beyond it, and the two reflections off the mirror dim the phantom. MirrorGuard identifies a phantom by these cues over multiple scans and removes the reflected beams before it reaches any detector or occupancy grid. On real-world recordings of this attack, MirrorGuard removes 96.31% of the phantom's returns at 98.30% precision, with 99.99% of non-phantom returns untouched. In a closed loop with the CARLA driving simulator and the open-source stack (Autoware), a vehicle without the defense halts for an obstacle that is not present and a following car crashes into its rear. With MirrorGuard, no vehicle produces a halt or a crash. MirrorGuard runs at 59 ms mean per scan on a CPU and is a software-only solution that does not require new hardware or environmental training.
items.title: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Perception against Passive Mirror Attacks

items.summary: Image inference on a shared CPU leaves input-dependent traces in software-visible performance counters and execution time. CHIP (Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection) trains a lightweight residual projector on public images to map these measurements into the 768-dimensional visual embedding space of a frozen OpenAI CLIP model. A frozen Stable unCLIP generator uses the projected embeddings to reconstruct recognizable color scenes for held-out inputs. The attack requires no physical probe, candidate image gallery, domain-specific generator, or shared cache, and elapsed time alone retains the signal. We evaluate full-counter, single-counter, and timing-only measurements on Intel Haswell and Sapphire Rapids. The projected embeddings achieve 0.85 ROC AUC for held-out image identification, compared with a 0.50 baseline. Exact-image top-five retrieval reaches 24% on CIFAR-100 and 56% on Unsafe-Diffusion. Across both processors, reconstructions average $1.4\times$ the baseline RGB color-palette overlap and $2.5\times$ the baseline structural similarity.
items.title: CHIP: Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection. Can OpenAI CLIP Reconstruct Images from the CPU Computational Footprint?

items.summary: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.
items.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling

items.summary: We design a lightweight authentication and key agreement protocol for Internet of Drones (IoD) environments that simultaneously provides post-quantum security, hardware-rooted trust, and resistance against machine-learning-based Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) modeling attacks. Existing PUF-based authentication schemes for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer protection against cloning and physical capture, but generally lack resistance against quantum adversaries. Conversely, recent post-quantum UAV authentication protocols provide quantum-resistant key establishment, yet do not incorporate hardware-bound authentication mechanisms and therefore remain vulnerable to device cloning and physical compromise. To address these limitations, we integrate CRYSTALS-Kyber, dynamic challenge scrambling (DCS), fuzzy extractors, and PUF-based identity binding into a unified framework. The resulting protocol enables anonymous authentication, forward secrecy, resistance to physical capture and replay attacks, and secure drone-to-drone communication, while maintaining suitability for resource-constrained UAV platforms. We provide a formal security analysis of the proposed scheme under the real-or-random model, a ProVerif-based formal verification, an informal analysis of its effectiveness against various attacks, and a performance evaluation of the proposed scheme through communication, computation, and storage cost analyses, which show its advantages over state-of-the-art architectures.
items.title: Quantum-Resilient, PUF-Based, and Anonymity-Preserving Authentication and Key Agreement Scheme for UAV Networks

items.summary: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.
items.title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones

items.summary: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.
items.title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
