items.summary: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
items.title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution

items.summary: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.
items.title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current

items.summary: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.
items.title: Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection

items.summary: Anomaly-based malicious traffic detection learns decision boundaries for normal behavior and identifies deviations as anomalies. However, normal behavior varies across networks and changes dynamically, limiting adaptability and increasing retraining costs. Despite this variability, our measurements show that clients accessing the same service exhibit consistent flow structures and interaction patterns, since each service provides specific functionality. We therefore construct service-specific decision boundaries. However, variations in personalized requests make it difficult to construct stable boundaries. To address this challenge, we propose IDSMorph, a self-adaptive malicious traffic detection system that learns consistency-guided embeddings through two key designs: (1) a flow structure consistency builder, which constructs contrastive samples capturing consistent embeddings within services; and (2) a service interaction consistency builder, which captures local structural consistency among different clients and global behavioral consistency among clients accessing that service. IDSMorph constructs dynamic decision boundaries from the majority of similar embeddings within each service and dynamically updates them through a differencing algorithm that mitigates the transient traffic shifts within short observation windows. Experiments show that IDSMorph's detection F1 score decreases by no more than 0.12 points across network environments, compared with an average decrease of 55.43 points for prior methods. In real-world deployment with red-team operators independently choosing attack strategies and timing, IDSMorph achieves an F1 score 46.81 points higher than other methods.
items.title: IDSMorph: Self-Adaptive Malicious Traffic Detection through Consistency-Guided Dynamic Decision Boundaries

items.summary: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.
items.title: Unshardable Codes

items.summary: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems can improve IoT security, but high-dimensional traffic features and imbalanced datasets may reduce model reliability and deployment feasibility in resource-constrained environments. This study presents a lightweight binary IoT intrusion detection framework using an approximately balanced CICIoT2023 derived dataset, feature reduction, and comparative machine learning evaluation. The original multi-class attack labels were converted into two classes: Benign and Malicious. To reduce class bias, malicious traffic was randomly undersampled to obtain an approximately balanced binary dataset. Information Gain Ratio and Gini Decrease were then used to rank traffic features and generate reduced feature subsets of 38, 30, 20, 10, 5, and 3 features. Five machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest(RF), Decision Tree(DT), Naive Bayes(NB), Logistic Regression(LR), and Support Vector Machine(SVM), were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that Random Forest achieved the strongest overall performance. In particular,the 20-feature subset achieved accuracy of 99.1% and MCC of 0.982, matching the full-feature model while reducing feature dimensionality by approximately 47.4%. The 10-feature subset also maintained strong performance with accuracy of 98.9% and MCC of 0.979, reducing the feature space by approximately 73.7%. These findings demonstrate that balanced binary classification and progressive feature reduction can preserve detection effectiveness while improving lightweight IDS feasibility.
items.title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Classifiers for Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection Using Feature Reduction

items.summary: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.
items.title: MobileGrail: Learning Compact Guardrails for On-Device deployable Mobile GUI Agent Safety

items.summary: Commercial AI agents increasingly incorporate long-term memory (both persistent and chat-history) to enable more accurate and personalized responses, raises significant privacy and policy concerns. Yet little is known about user privacy risks associated with memory behavior, in particular, about memory storage, disclosure, transparency and deletion control. To bridge this gap, we propose FORGETMENOT, an auditing framework for analyzing the privacy risks of long term memory in commercial AI agents. Using our framework, we collect around 3800 multi-turn sessions comprising around 6M tokens across five popular AI agents. Our results show that agents store a wide range of personal attributes, including demographics, health, and sensitive details. Furthermore, user visible memory reveals substantially less (around 20% on average) attributes than the agents store in practice, exposing a significant transparency gap. Our stealth memory injection (SMI) technique further increases the amount of personal and sensitive attribute stored in memory, raising it by 25% and 15% for Copilot and Claude, respectively. We further observed memory deletion control is unreliable, as all five agents exhibit non-zero post deletion leakage, including health and self-harm related attributes. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of memory disclosure to a 3rd-party email recipient as a proof-of-concept, as Gemini shows 31.9% leakage rate. Together, our findings reveal notable privacy risks in commercial agents memory. Finally, we discuss both design implications and regulatory recommendations to protect users memory privacy in commercial agents.
items.title: FORGETMENOT: Auditing Memory Driven Privacy Risks in Commercial AI Agents

items.summary: The evolving cellular networks continue to rely on the legacy GPRS Tunneling Protocol-User Plane (GTP-U) to encapsulate and route user data traffic across the data plane. Recent security research demonstrated that nested GTP-U (GTP-in-GTP) payload vulnerabilities enable a diverse range of attacks on victim users. To address this vulnerability, in this paper, we propose a closed-loop extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and eXpress Data Path (XDP) defense to detect and mitigate nested GTP-U attacks in 5G and beyond networks. The proposed framework contains three components: an in-kernel XDP Detection and Drop Module (XDP-DDM), a user-space User-Plane Telemetry Agent (UP-TA), and a multi-threaded Control-Plane Mitigation Orchestrator (CP-MO). We implement and evaluate the proposed defense on a sliced 5G testbed integrating Free5GC, UERANSIM, and Containerlab. Experimental results indicate that the XDP-DDM detects and drops malicious nested GTP-U packets at line rate, while the UP-TA and CP-MO asynchronously report and revoke the attacker's network access, respectively. Under a 10,000 packets-per-second cross-slice nested GTP-U flood, the proposed solution preserves the baseline performance of the victim slices while introducing minimal overhead. items.summary: Backdoor attacks pose a significant security threat to deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on AI inference engines and hardware accelerators. By embedding hidden triggers during training, these attacks induce malicious behavior while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. Multi-trigger backdoor attacks are particularly challenging to detect and mitigate because of the distributed and stealthy nature of their effects. items.summary: Computing point-to-point shortest paths in large weighted graphs can require classical algorithms to explore a substantial portion of the graph. We ask whether quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) can reduce the work required to return a verified shortest path. For a known set of queries, we select paths that share arcs. For new queries, we select a corridor and test whether any path leaving it could improve the distance found by Dijkstra's algorithm. We also partition the graph into blocks and reuse local paths between their boundaries. We compare path encodings on identical inputs using simulated annealing on classical processors. The comparison of exact block overlays with direct Dijkstra search covered 45 synthetic graphs and the New York road network with 264,346 vertices. The overlay reduced the number of arc inspections in the final search in 97 of 200 graph and block-size combinations. Once endpoint attachment, assembly, and reconstruction were included, every combination took longer per query than direct Dijkstra search. On a separate set of 168 synthetic graphs, tightening the flow penalty increased the fraction of trials returning a verified local optimum within 20,ms from 35.8% to 84.1% under the same annealing schedule and update policy. A cost model for a prepared graph of 16,384 vertices predicts a 1.072x query speedup over a parallel classical overlay if five local problems can be solved accurately in one batch at the assumed service cost. The practical benefit of reduction thus depends on whether savings in the final search cover the cost of obtaining and verifying the local paths.

items.summary: Face verification systems are deployed by selecting a decision threshold that achieves a target false match rate (FMR); performance is then reported as the corresponding false non-match rate (FNMR). Prior work (Wu et al., 2024) measures the resulting optimistic bias as a small additive change in 10-fold accuracy (up to 1.01 percentage points). Manual review of 100 flagged IJB-C subjects confirms 69.2%, implying a residual overlap of roughly 9.9%. items.summary: High-dimensional quantum key distribution tolerates more noise than qubit-based protocols, but the dimension that maximizes the secret key depends on turbulence, background light, device imperfections, and block size, all of which change during an airborne or satellite pass. Finite-size security analyses of high-dimensional protocols fix the dimension in advance, and the dimension-adaptive schemes reported so far have been analyzed only asymptotically. Here, a controller sets the dimension, acceptance thresholds, and key length of each block using only public data from earlier blocks. Each block is therefore a standard fixed-length protocol, and composable finite-key security against coherent attacks follows from sequential composition; an inaccurate channel model reduces the key rate but does not weaken security. The controller estimates turbulence from observed error rates, maximizes the expected key under forecast uncertainty, and recalibrates its model online. We evaluate it on a simulated entanglement-based orbital-angular-momentum link between an aircraft and a ground station, using Kolmogorov phase screens and the Hufnagel--Valley turbulence profile. Accounting for forecast uncertainty increases the key by 31\%--47\% relative to a naive planner. Over night, dawn, daytime, and model-mismatch scenarios, the recalibrated controller retains at least 98.8\% of the key obtained with the best fixed dimension for each scenario, while every fixed dimension drops to 73.5\% or less in at least one scenario. Running the link's measurement statistics on a superconducting quantum processor shows device errors close to a constant offset; with these errors included, the best daytime dimension changes from eight to four, and the controller adjusts accordingly.

items.summary: Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under $SO(3)$ viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group ($\mathcal{I}_{60}$) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of $SO(3)$, we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous $SO(3)$ rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.
items.title: RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images

items.summary: Decoding both uplink and downlink cellular traffic reveals lower-layer protocol behavior, unprotected signaling, and encrypted higher-layer packets beyond what scheduling metadata exposes. In commercial 5G NR networks, however, passive decoding must overcome UE-dedicated configurations hidden in encrypted signaling, unknown identifiers of ongoing connections, and the computational demands of wideband traffic. We present NRSnooper, a passive sniffer that decodes downlink control and bidirectional data traffic in real time, including traffic from already-connected UEs and traffic after encrypted configuration updates. NRSnooper learns reusable physical-layer configurations through an instrumented open-source UE that reproduces commercial UE capabilities. It recovers connection-specific identifiers from ongoing transmissions and selects matching configurations through CRC-validated data decoding. A hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline sustains continuous wideband processing. Evaluations on a controlled testbed and two commercial networks show that, compared with using only configurations from unencrypted signaling, NRSnooper decodes 1.3x and 6.3x as many control messages and 9.0x and 17.7x as many downlink data blocks, respectively. NRSnooper also decodes traffic from an already-connected UE during an ongoing phone call and achieves real-time bidirectional decoding on 100 MHz commercial NR channels.

items.summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted data, but its substantial computational cost hinders adoption in privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Neural processing units (NPUs) already deployed in AI infrastructure provide a practical platform for FHE acceleration. However, after mapping the number theoretic transform (NTT) to matrix multiplications on Ascend NPUs, modular arithmetic and representation conversion on the Vector backend still incur substantial overhead at stage boundaries. Evaluation-key material of key switching also increases storage and data-transfer costs, and whole-limb task assignment causes tail load imbalance. We present NPUFHE, an end-to-end CKKS execution system optimized for Ascend NPUs. To reduce modular recovery and twiddle costs in NTT, we propose Boundary-Optimized NTT, which eliminates intra-axis modular recovery, compiles intra-axis twiddle factors into matrix constants, and introduces two-level folded modular recovery at axis endpoints. To alleviate evaluation-key storage and transfer pressure, we design Compact Shoup encoding, which halves the key representation through local coefficient recovery. Finally, we propose Cost-Aware Parallel Tiling to mitigate tail load imbalance caused by whole-limb task assignment. It uses a cost model to adaptively partition tail tasks and smooth stepwise latency increases. We integrate the above designs into OpenFHE. On one Ascend 910B4, full-packing CKKS bootstrapping with real evaluation keys takes 0.95 s, encrypted CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 inference with bootstrapping requires 9.87 s per image, and encrypted MNIST inference achieves an amortized latency of 19.81 ms per image. The peak NTT throughput of NPUFHE reaches up to $184.22\times$, $2.04\times$, and $4.46\times$ that of OpenFHE on CPU, TensorFHE, and CROSS, respectively.
items.title: NPUFHE: An Efficient CKKS Execution System for Ascend NPUs

items.summary: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.
items.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection

items.summary: Confidential GPUs offer near-native on-device compute performance, but transfers between CPU and GPU TEEs through untrusted host memory require bulk CPU encryption and decryption, even for unchanged data. Existing software techniques overlap or parallelize these operations but retain their per-byte CPU cost. Reusing exported ciphertext could avoid this work, but GPU TEE firmware enforces direction-specific encryption keys and fresh per-transfer initialization vectors (IVs), preventing direct reuse. We introduce ciphertext rebinding, a purely software primitive enabling repeated and cross-GPU ciphertext reuse on existing GPU TEEs without hardware changes, while preserving confidentiality, integrity, and freshness. Specifically, ciphertext rebinding exploits the separation between ciphertext-dependent and IV-dependent components in GPU TEE's AES-GCM authentication: a GPU-precomputed summary under the destination key can enable the CPU to update authentication tags without processing the payload. With this modification, GPU's subsequent read on the retained ciphertext can still proceed through the GPU's hardware-fixed copy-engine interfaces, which cannot be modified by software. An additional GPU correction step can then compensate for differences in the keys and IVs to recover the original plaintext. By retaining GPU-exported ciphertext in untrusted host memory, ciphertext rebinding avoids bulk CPU decryption and re-encryption, improving effective bandwidth for GPU-state restoration and sharing. We implement this primitive in HiPerfCC-StateReuse through only driver and library changes, combining batched submissions with pipelined GPU processing and copy-engine transfers. We evaluate transfer efficiency and CPU overhead through microbenchmarks, and application performance through three case studies: model switching, key-value cache offloading, and cross-instance cache sharing.

The resulting monitor, Q-TRACE (Quantum Telemetry Residuals Against Calibrated Expectations), calibrates a physical model of each link on commissioning data, profiles out the transmittance, and combines omnibus residual, physics score and setting-allocation tests with drift-robust references; no attack data are used. The formulation also yields a detectability exponent D* that lower-bounds the delay of any telemetry monitor and vanishes for a Trojan-horse probe with filtered back-reflection. Its delay attains the bound for strongly detectable attacks. On 33 parallel BB84 links of the IBM Heron processor ibm_marrakesh with physically executed entangling and amplitude-damping eavesdroppers, the measured information-disturbance relations agree with theory; a commissioning reference acquired under different operating conditions triggers alarms in every monitor tested, while a condition-matched reference detects a probe with 0.3% ideal QBER increase on 14 of 14 link-epochs with no false alarm on 66 honest ones.

items.summary: AI agents call external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Some MCP servers return paid advertisements (ads) into the model's context. The model then decides whether these ads and their disclosures reach the user. We trace these ads from their sources to the agent's tool results across public MCP servers and packages. We find the servers through their public traces in ad networks, package registries, certificate logs, hostnames, MCP directories, and GitHub configurations. We then query the ad-serving servers with read-only requests and inspect their ad links. Ads appear on only 0.57% of 101,363 open MCP endpoints and 0.04% of 122,656 local MCP packages. Although 173 ad networks target agents, operators insert the ads themselves on about half of the 226 ad-returning servers. Nearly all ad-serving packages likewise carry the operator's own affiliate identifier. While ads adapt to the topic and intent of the query, their disclosure stays fixed within each tool. Only 9.3% of the ads carry an explicit sponsored label. Most ad links also hide their destinations. Since operators insert most ads themselves and label them inconsistently, we propose a per-item ad annotation in MCP results. Clients can show this annotation to the user independently of the model's answer.
items.title: Ads for Agents: Measuring Ad-Serving MCP Servers

items.summary: Static malware detectors that represent each sample as a bag of extracted features, such as permissions, API calls, or imported functions, are cheap to deploy and remain state-of-the-art under temporal drift and in selective classification. Yet, attackers can evade them by adding benign-looking content that outweighs malicious evidence. Canonically, detectors encode the presence of a few thousand features, selected during training, as sparse multi-hot vectors over a fixed vocabulary. Features that emerge after training remain invisible. We show that linear models and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) over this input are sum-pooled set models in disguise. Sum-pooling lets added benign features cancel malicious evidence. Instead, we cast malware detection with set-shaped static features as a multiple-instance learning (MIL) problem. To this end, we propose MalSets, which uses max-pooled Deep Sets models with a monotone head to ensure that any malicious evidence remains undiluted; thus, more is never less. Under MIL, a general text encoder maps any feature string to an embedding, thus eliminating the long-standing out-of-vocabulary problem at test time. Max-pooling retains the malicious evidence regardless of how many benign features an attacker adds. Since max-pooling can only grow when features are added, constraining the head alone makes the malware score monotone under additions, even against a white-box attacker adapted to this architecture. While monotone detectors are never evaded by state-of-the-art black-box or white-box attacks, they often significantly pay for this robustness in clean performance since benign features cannot count as evidence. However, by combining a non-monotone set encoder with max-pooling and a monotone head, MalSets maintains the robustness of prior monotone classifiers while achieving state-of-the-art performance.
items.title: More Is Never Less: Affordable Robustness to Additive Attacks via Monotone Multiple-Instance Learning

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.
items.title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design

items.summary: The large value $\varepsilon=19.61$, reported as an approximate differential privacy (ADP) parameter for the 2020 U.S. Census, has prompted doubts about the adequacy of Census privacy protection. It was obtained by converting component zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) guarantees to ADP at $δ=10^{-10}$. A single ADP pair can substantially loosen the original upper bound on the power (true positive rate) of a distinguishing test. At significance level $α$, we express the original bound as the smallest pure differential privacy (DP) parameter giving the same power bound. We call this the $α$-operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$. The full curve represents the original bound exactly on $(0,1)$, even when the bound is nonconcave. For maximum-power curves and bounds derived from trade-off functions, we characterize the extrema of operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ over an interval of significance levels. When finite, they give the parameters of the pure DP bounds that enclose the original power bound on that interval. The mapping preserves the ordering of power bounds at each significance level. For Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with equal noise variance, conversion to single ADP pairs or Gaussian DP envelopes can reverse this ordering. For the P.L. 94-171 redistricting data, we reproduce the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$ as the sum of rounded component ADP values. The published zCDP guarantee yields operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ values of approximately 4.25, 2.94, and 3.18 at significance levels of 1%, 5%, and 10%, respectively. Converting the same guarantee to a single ADP pair at $δ=10^{-10}$ gives power bounds near 1 at all three levels. The pure DP scale thus clarifies constraints on distinguishing attacks that are difficult to discern from the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$.
items.title: Reporting Differential Privacy Guarantees via Operationally Equivalent $\varepsilon$: What Does $\varepsilon=19.61$ Mean for the 2020 U.S. Census?

items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.
items.title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG

items.summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.
items.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers

items.summary: QR-UOV is a Quotient Ring Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) multivariate quadratic (MQ) signature scheme that has progressed to round-3 of the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) additional signatures call by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Until now, for architectural efficiency and performance trade-offs, QR-UOV has been evaluated only on software platforms and has never been considered on hardware, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). To address this, we are the first to provide a complete QR-UOV hardware implementation through a flexible and unified QUISA coprocessor design, which supports instruction-driven execution for key generation, signing, and verification across all three NIST security levels (SL-I, SL-III, SL-V). The proposed architecture features extensive throughput optimizations by parallelizing key QR-UOV module operations, such as the pseudorandom byte generator, hashing, and rejection sampling. To minimize hardware resources, we propose a modular arithmetic unit with finite-field reduction based on the shift-add folding method. The design introduces a linear system solver for QUISA based on LU decomposition with partial pivoting and a sample solution module, operating over the prime field Fq (q = 127). We comprehensively evaluate QUISA on an Artix-7 FPGA at 80 MHz up to the post-place-and-route stage, utilizing 11,144 slices and 35,248 look-up tables. For higher SL-V security levels, it completes key generation, signing, and verification in 30.4M, 3.8M, and 2.8M clock cycles, respectively.
items.title: QUISA: A Compact, Flexible and Unified Instruction-Set Coprocessor for QR-UOV Signature

items.summary: Tor end-to-end correlation attacks can link a client to its destination by matching traffic observed at both ends of a Tor circuit. However, their practical threat remains unclear for two reasons: existing correlation methods rely on O(N^2) pairwise processing, and prior works do not reflect the flow counts and base rates seen by realistic adversaries. We present InstantCoFFEA, which replaces exhaustive pairwise search with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval using CAGRA and introduces ranked voting. At N = 200k, InstantCoFFEA is 14.56x faster than DeepCoFFEA and improves PR-AUC from 0.94 to 0.96. We also use TorPS to estimate the flow counts and matching-pair base rates observed by relay-level and network-level adversaries. Our simulations show that realistic attacks involve substantially more candidate flows and much lower base rates than those used in prior evaluations. Under a low-base-rate setting, PR-AUC drops for all methods, but InstantCoFFEA achieves 0.53 compared with 0.42 for DeepCoFFEA. These results show that evaluating correlation attacks requires considering both computational scale and the sparsity of true matching pairs.
items.title: InstantCoFFEA: Fast and accurate Tor flow correlation at realistic scale

items.summary: In 2001 we published a paper on an Anti OS Detection (AoD) system: a modified FreeBSD 4.3 kernel that makes a host answer the probes of an OS fingerprinting tool as if it ran another operating system. This report revisits that work on FreeBSD 15.1. We do not claim a new method. We report three things. First, the same goal is now reachable from a loadable module of about 800 lines that uses the packet filter hook interface and sets one kernel variable, without changing the kernel source. Second, the module covers both active and passive fingerprinting: Nmap 7.98 reports an exact match for Linux and for Windows 10/11, and p0f 3 reports the same systems from the connections the host opens. Third, an exact match in Nmap was not enough: a passive tool, plain FIN scans and a comparison with real hosts each exposed a mismatch that the previous step could not see. A real Windows 11 host and the final Windows personality get the same verdict from Nmap and the same signatures from p0f and JA4T; a real Linux 7.0 host is not an exact match in Nmap at all, while the personality built from Nmap's database is. We describe those mismatches, how we removed them, what the module costs, and what it still cannot hide.
items.title: Anti OS Fingerprinting, Revisited: A Loadable Kernel Module for FreeBSD and What Twenty-Five Years Changed

items.summary: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes numerical values as probabilistic bit-streams and enables arithmetic operations using simple logic gates, offering a promising paradigm for low- cost, fault-tolerant, and highly parallel computation. However, the accuracy and efficiency of SC systems depend on the quality of the stochastic number generator (SNG). Conventional SNGs rely on pseudo-random or quasi-random generators, whose deterministic nature introduces periodicity, correlation, and bias, limiting achievable accuracy and robustness. This paper proposes a low- cost arbiter physical unclonable function (APUF)-based SNG that operates in near-metastable delay conditions to generate true- random stochastic bit-streams with controllable output probabilities. By selecting input challenges that drive the path delay difference toward a target value, the resulting output probability is governed by intrinsic device noise, eliminating the need for conventional random-number generators and comparator-based SNGs. The proposed design inherits the low hardware overhead and statistical independence properties of the APUF structure. A probabilistic model and a challenge selection method are developed to characterize and control the stochastic behavior. An 8-stage APUF-SNG matches the 1% mean absolute error of state- of-the-art true-random SNGs at 1024-bit streams and occupies 116μm^2 in 45nm, 2.5x and 7x smaller than the TRNG-based and Sobol-based generator designs, respectively.
items.title: APUF-SNG: A Low-Cost Arbiter-PUF Stochastic Number Generator with Tunable Output Probability

items.summary: Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation's parameters. Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{λ/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $λ$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.
items.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP

items.summary: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.
items.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning

items.summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. items.summary: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.
items.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications

items.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.
items.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study

items.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.
items.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models

items.summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

items.summary: Machine learning (ML) property attestation lets a model provider demonstrate properties of their models and datasets to verifiers, and trusted execution environments (TEEs) have emerged as its most practical mechanism. However, existing TEE-based systems attest only a static snapshot of the TEE's initial configuration, leaving run-time behavior unauditable. Proof of execution (PoX) architectures close this gap by requiring the prover's root of trust to also demonstrate that (1) the attested operation actually executed and (2) the claimed outputs were affected only by that operation. Existing PoX designs, though, target microcontrollers and rely on hardware features unavailable in server-grade TEEs, so they cannot be applied directly to ML workloads. We present EVOLVE, a software-based PoX framework for server-grade TEEs. EVOLVE mediates an operation's writes and control flow to track whether a requested ML operation executes without violation. It binds the execution status to measurements of the operation's inputs and outputs, enabling verifiers to assess run-time behavior through ML property attestation. We implement EVOLVE on Intel TDX as a Rust module within its virtual firmware, with policy checks built on primitives formally verified in F*. Our evaluation shows that EVOLVE is versatile across diverse ML applications on unmodified hardware, provides formal guarantees for its policy checks. EVOLVE incurs per-request run-time overhead on average ranging from 1.07$\times$ (for decision trees) to 2.13$\times$ (for multi-layer perceptrons).
items.title: Enabling Verifiable Output Lineage for Virtualized ML Workload Execution

items.summary: A software-defined vehicle depends on products that sit under different EU regimes. The type-approved vehicle and the systems, components and separate technical units made for it fall under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, which makes UN R155 mandatory; Regulation (EU) 2018/858 does so for R156; and ISO/SAE 21434 supports the management system R155 requires. Chargers, companion apps, aftermarket devices and many backends may fall under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) instead, whose reporting duty in Article 14 has applied since 11 September 2026. Neither side defines how a vulnerability found on one reaches the other's risk process. We contribute a four-question classification procedure, a five-regime traceability matrix, a reference architecture with four handoff paths and three boundary findings. On 75 classified products from a frozen public-source corpus, the procedure yields 47 Periphery, 11 Core, 1 Other and 16 Boundary products, three of them outside both the CRA and compulsory R155. Because UN R10 lets an electronic sub-assembly be approved as a component, the texts leave a second reading open, and we report both counts. Under it, 22 aftermarket devices become components, Periphery falls to 25 and 25 products sit outside both regimes. Seven retrospective walkthroughs suggest that, for third-party products, vulnerability information stops in the vehicle manufacturer's own inventory, triggers or exploitation assessment, and that no provision obliges a product maker to tell a vehicle manufacturer: the only defined two-way route is a contract. No reviewed source establishes a case that reached an Article 14 clock.

items.summary: Phishing remains one of the most pervasive and damaging cyber threats, exploiting both technical flaws and human behavior to compromise sensitive data. We present a privacy-preserving, real-time defense that analyzes full webpage source code on mobile platforms. Our system combines a lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for end-to-end feature extraction with a Federated Learning (FL) framework that updates models collaboratively on user devices without transferring raw data-supporting regulatory compliance and personalization. Evaluated on a large and diverse dataset, the model attains 86.02\% accuracy, 90.35\% precision, 80.64\% recall, and 92.78\% ROC-AUC. While some centralized, classical approaches may report higher accuracy, our design emphasizes a practical balance among accuracy, user privacy, and real-time performance on resource-constrained devices. We further demonstrate an end-to-end integration within the open-source Lightning Android browser, achieving real-time detection with low computational overhead. This work shows that privacy-first, AI-driven phishing detection is both feasible and scalable across mobile and IoT settings, delivering robust protection while keeping user data on-device.
items.title: Development of an Effective Federated Learning-Based Defense System Against Phishing Attacks on Mobile Platforms

items.summary:
The fix for CVE-2026-45756 lowers pcre.backtrack_limit to 10000 around each preg_match() call of the match() and search() filter functions. That limit applies to one starting position, not to one call. PCRE resets its counter at every position it tries a match from. So an unanchored pattern that stays just under the limit is paid once per byte of the subject. Each call also starts from a fresh limit, so chaining clauses in one filter multiplies the work.

Two other paths made the cost of a query grow faster than its size, without any regular expression:
- The filter evaluator scanned the whole expression for logical operators once per node. Its cost grew with the square of the number of chained clauses.
- Queries starting with $ inside a filter, like @.x == $.limit or length($.items), were evaluated again for every node the filter visits.

An application that evaluates an attacker-influenced JSONPath expression can therefore still be made to hold a PHP worker. A document of 2 MB and a query of 2.5 KB take 3.5 minutes of CPU.

JsonCrawler::find() now bounds the total regex work of one call, and throws an exception when that budget is exhausted. Filter expressions are parsed once per query, and absolute queries inside filters are evaluated once per query.

items.summary:
Most methods of Symfony\Component\Filesystem\Path rely on Path::split(), which takes everything before the first :// as the root of a path. It doesn't check that this prefix is a URI scheme, so the .. segments in that prefix are never resolved. PHP sees a scheme only at the start of a string. So /base/../x://../secret.txt is a plain local path to /secret.txt for PHP, while Path::isBasePath('/base', '/base/../x://../secret.txt') returns true. canonicalize(), join(), makeAbsolute() and makeRelative() are affected the same way.

Some applications check a path built from user input with isBasePath() or canonicalize(), and then open it. They can be made to read or write files outside the expected directory.

On Symfony 6.4 and later, the AssetMapper component builds with Path::join() the path of the files that a remote package references from its CSS. A malicious or compromised package can therefore make importmap:require or importmap:install write a file of its choice outside assets/vendor. For example, the CSS url(../../../../../public/x://shell.php) writes public/x:/shell.php.

A prefix is now a scheme only when PHP would look for a stream wrapper with that name. That is two or more letters, digits, +, - or ., followed by :// at the start of the path. Other prefixes are regular path segments, and the .. segments after them are resolved. Real schemes such as phar://, file://, vfs:// or compress.zlib:// keep working.

items.summary: Reliance on an untrusted source of the client address in the WebSocket listener of the NetBird relay server (relay/server/listener/ws) in NetBird versions 0.31.1 through 0.74.7 allows an attacker with an enrolled peer to spoof the source address of their relay connection. The listener used the values of the X-Real-Ip and X-Real-Port request headers as the remote address of the connection unconditionally, without checking that the request came from a trusted upstream proxy. A WebSocket client that sends both headers makes the relay record and use an arbitrary address for its connection, including in the relay connection log, so a client can hide its real address or attribute its connection to another host. Only the relay server is affected; the NetBird client, including the Android and iOS apps, does not run the relay listener. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which honours these headers only for requests whose direct connection address is in a configured set of trusted proxies and ignores them by default.

items.summary: Binding to an unrestricted IP address in the netstack SOCKS5 proxy of the NetBird client (client/iface/netstack) in NetBird versions before 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated attacker on the same network as the client to relay traffic through the client into its NetBird overlay network. When the client runs in netstack mode (NB_USE_NETSTACK_MODE=true), it starts a SOCKS5 proxy, without authentication, that is meant to bridge applications on the local host into the userspace WireGuard stack. The listener was bound to 0.0.0.0 instead of the loopback address, so any host that can reach the proxy port (1080 by default) can connect and reach peers and internal resources with the network position of the affected client. Netstack mode is not enabled by default. The issue is fixed in version 0.74.7, which binds the proxy to 127.0.0.1 by default.

items.summary: Deserialization of untrusted data in the relay server handshake of NetBird versions 0.29.0 through 0.74.7 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to reach the Go encoding/gob decoder with attacker-supplied bytes before any credential is checked, which can lead to denial of service of the relay server. The deprecated Hello handshake message was still accepted before authentication and its token was decoded with gob.NewDecoder (shared/relay/auth/hmac) before the HMAC signature was verified. The handshake buffer limits the input to 212 bytes and the pre-authentication phase to 10 seconds, so there is no impact on confidentiality or integrity and the impact on availability depends on a separate weakness in the gob decoder of the Go toolchain used to build the relay server, such as CVE-2024-34156. The Auth handshake, used by clients since version 0.29.1, does not use gob. The issue is fixed in version 0.75.0, which removes the Hello handshake and the gob-based token decoding.

items.summary:
In Eclipse BaSyx Java Server SDK versions 2.0.0-milestone-10 to 2.0.0-milestone-16, the destination validation of the Operation Delegation feature, introduced to prevent server-side request forgery (CVE-2026-7412), can be bypassed through DNS rebinding.



Before dispatching a delegated Operation invocation, the server resolves the host of the `invocationDelegation` qualifier URI and rejects loopback, private, link-local, multicast and cloud metadata addresses. The outbound HTTP client (Reactor Netty), however, performs its own, independent DNS lookup when opening the connection and does not use the validated addresses. An attacker who can create or update a Submodel Operation and controls the DNS records of the delegation host can answer the validation lookup with a public address and the connection lookup with an internal address. No authentication is required when the authorization feature is not enabled.



Invoking the Operation then causes the BaSyx server to send HTTP POST requests to destinations the protection is meant to block, such as services in internal IT/OT networks, loopback-only interfaces, or cloud metadata endpoints. The server can be used to pivot into network segments that are not directly reachable by the attacker.



Only deployments with the Operation Delegation feature enabled are affected. The feature is enabled by default.



The issue is fixed in Eclipse BaSyx Java Server SDK 2.0.0-milestone-17.

When bv_len is 0 or 1, the subtraction wraps to a large value which is then truncated to uint16_t, yielding 0xFFFE (65534) or 0xFFFF (65535). The module constructs HTTP requests to the Vonage/Nexmo SMS API by encoding
API credentials (api_key and api_secret) into URL query parameters and
sending them via GET requests. This causes credentials to be exposed in web

the victim's Vonage/Nexmo account.

items.summary:
Module: plugins/modules/keyring_info.py 

CVSS 3.1: 5.5 MEDIUM — AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N 

Issue: The module retrieves a passphrase from the OS native keyring (GNOME Keyring, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager) and places it directly into result["passphrase"] with no output suppression, no no_log protection, and no documentation warning. 

Root Cause:

Line 105 (protected): keyring_password=dict(type="str", required=True, no_log=True)
Line 127 (NOT protected): result["passphrase"] = passphrase

Observed Output:

{
"changed": false,
"passphrase": "MyMasterP@ssw0rd!SSH_Key_Secret"
}
Visible via register + debug:
{
"keyring_result": {
"changed": false,
"passphrase": "MyMasterP@ssw0rd!SSH_Key_Secret"
}
}

Impact: 

Master passwords, SSH key passphrases and service credentials appear in all Ansible output 

register: keyring_result followed by debug: var=keyring_result prints passphrase in full 

Ansible fact caching backends (Redis, JSON file, memcached) may persist the passphrase 

AWX/Tower job logs silently store the live credential

Fix:

module.exit_json(changed=False, passphrase=passphrase, _ansible_no_log=True)

Also add a documentation warning requiring callers to use no_log: true at the task level.

PoCs


Fig 1: PoC execution showing passphrase in plaintext output


Fig 2: Source code showing no_log=True on input (line 105) vs unprotected output (line 127)

items.summary:
The @symfony/stimulus-bridge npm package includes a Webpack loader called lazy-controller-loader that supports "magic comments" placed above a Stimulus controller import, for example /* stimulusFetch: 'lazy' */, to control lazy loading behavior. To read those options, the loader extracted the raw text of any stimulus* comment and evaluated it as JavaScript using Node's vm.runInNewContext(). The Node.js node:vm module is not a security sandbox, and a crafted comment can break out of the VM context using well-known techniques to run arbitrary Node.js code within the build process.

This is a build-time vulnerability: it does not affect browsers or end users. The code executes on the developer machine or CI/build server during a Webpack or Symfony Encore build. Realistic attack vectors include a malicious Stimulus controller introduced through a compromised dependency, or a pull request that triggers an automated CI build. An attacker who can get such a file into the build can read files and environment variables available to the build process, exfiltrate CI secrets, tamper with generated build artifacts, and run commands with the permissions of the build user.

The loader no longer evaluates comment content as JavaScript. It now parses each comment as an object expression using a real JavaScript parser and extracts only plain literal values. Any non-literal value, such as a function call, an identifier, or a sequence expression, is rejected and reported as a build error instead of being executed. Legitimate option values like 'lazy' and 'eager' continue to work without any changes required on the user's side.

items.summary:
A live component protected by #[IsGranted], on its class or on its default action, can be rendered by a caller who is not granted access. POST /_components/{name}/_batch is handled by Symfony\UX\LiveComponent\Controller\BatchActionController, which has no controller attributes: the attributes of the component are only checked by the sub-request issued for each action. With an empty actions list, no sub-request was issued, and the hydrated component was rendered and returned with a 200.

The caller needs a valid signed props payload for the component, such as the data-live-props-value of a page that rendered it: one the caller could see before losing access, or a cached or shared page. The checksum binds the props to the component name, not to a user, a session or a time, so such a payload can be replayed. Actions are not affected, since each action of a non-empty batch is still checked in its own sub-request. Components that load data from their props, like an entity identifier, disclose that data to the caller.

BatchActionController now rejects a batch without any action with a BadRequestHttpException. The JavaScript client never sends such a request: it uses the URL of the component when there is no action, /{action} for a single one and /_batch for two or more.

items.summary:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input in ZenHive mpp allows an unauthenticated remote client to drain the fee-payer wallet in a single request by naming an arbitrarily high gas price.

When the mpp Elixir library is configured as fee payer (fee_payer: true), MPP.Tempo.Transaction.cosign_fee_payer/3 re-signs the client-supplied base fields of the 0x76 AASigned envelope verbatim, including max_fee_per_gas and max_priority_fee_per_gas, without validating that they are within reasonable bounds. A malicious client embeds arbitrarily large values for these fields in the signed envelope. The server co-signs and broadcasts the transaction. The effective_gas_price billed against the fee-payer wallet is derived from the attacker-supplied ceilings, so the server pays those inflated per-gas rates out of its own wallet. A single crafted request can drain the wallet entirely, after which the server can no longer sponsor gas for legitimate payment requests.

This issue affects mpp: from 0.2.0 before 0.6.0.

items.summary:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input in ZenHive mpp allows an unauthenticated remote client to inflate the fee-payer's gas cost per payment by a large multiplier, degrading the sponsor's operating margin.

When the mpp Elixir library is configured as fee payer (fee_payer: true), MPP.Tempo.Transaction.cosign_fee_payer/3 re-signs the client-supplied base fields of the 0x76 AASigned envelope verbatim, including the EIP-2930 access list, without validating its length or contents. EIP-2930 access list entries incur intrinsic gas (~2,400 gas per address, plus 1,900 gas per storage key) charged before any opcode executes, regardless of whether the listed addresses are ever touched. A malicious client submits a valid transferWithMemo call alongside a large number of fabricated access-list entries. The server co-signs and broadcasts the transaction. The intended transfer executes normally, but the fee-payer wallet pays a large multiple of the expected gas cost with no corresponding on-chain work.

At the maintainer's default of 137 access-list entries (fitting within Bandit's 10,000-byte per-header-field limit) and 100 Gwei max_fee_per_gas, per-payment gas cost rises from ~51,287 to ~380,087 gas, a 7.4x multiplier. items.summary:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input in ZenHive mpp allows an unauthenticated remote client to drain the fee-payer wallet, resulting in denial of service for legitimate clients.

When the mpp Elixir library is configured as fee payer (fee_payer: true), the MPP.Methods.Tempo payment method co-signs and broadcasts a client-supplied EVM transaction without first validating that the client-supplied gas_limit is sufficient to complete the intended call. A malicious client can submit a signed transferWithMemo transaction with gas_limit deliberately set just below the amount required for successful execution. The server co-signs the transaction and broadcasts it via rpc_broadcast_sync. The transaction runs out of gas during EVM execution and reverts, but the fee-payer wallet is still charged for the burned gas while the client pays nothing and receives no resource. Repeated requests from one or more malicious clients drain the fee-payer wallet at near-zero cost to the attacker, ultimately preventing the server from sponsoring gas for legitimate payment requests.

The wait_for_confirmation = false (optimistic) path is also affected: it invokes simulate_payment_call via eth_call, but that simulation omits the gas parameter and therefore does not catch out-of-gas conditions.

This issue affects mpp: from 0.2.0 before 0.6.0.

items.summary:
Inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests (HTTP response smuggling) vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a malicious HTTP/1 server to desynchronize a strict intermediary and the Mint client on the same pooled connection, enabling response-queue poisoning against subsequent requests that share the connection.

The Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5 function in lib/mint/http1.ex parses the chunk-size line of a Transfer-Encoding: chunked response with Integer.parse(data, 16). RFC 7230 defines chunk-size = 1*HEXDIG and forbids any sign prefix, but Integer.parse/2 accepts an optional leading + or -. A chunk-size line of +5 is accepted as a five-byte chunk; lines of +0 and -0 are accepted as the terminating zero-length chunk and end the message body early.

An RFC-strict intermediary in the response path rejects these forms, so the intermediary and the Mint client disagree on where one response ends and the next begins. On a pooled keep-alive connection, an attacker-influenced origin can inject bytes that the client attributes to the next legitimate response on the same connection, poisoning the response queue and corrupting the responses returned to unrelated in-flight requests.

This issue affects mint: from 0.1.0 before 1.9.3.

items.summary:
Allocation of resources without limits vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a remote HTTP server to exhaust memory on the client host and cause a denial of service.

The Mint.HTTP1.decode_headers/5 and Mint.HTTP1.decode_trailer_headers/4 functions in lib/mint/http1.ex accumulate every parsed response header and chunked-trailer field into a per-request list that persists across incoming TCP segments as request.headers_buffer, and only clear it when the terminating blank line is received. The section has no cap on the number of headers or on total bytes, and the underlying :erlang.decode_packet(:httph_bin, binary, []) parser is invoked with an empty option list so its per-line and per-packet size limits also default to unlimited.

A malicious HTTP server (reachable directly, via an attacker-controlled redirect, via SSRF, or via a man-in-the-middle) can stream complete header lines (or, after a chunked body, complete trailer lines) indefinitely without ever emitting the terminating blank line. The connection state grows without bound until the BEAM node is killed by the operating system's out-of-memory handler, taking down the entire application that uses Mint as an HTTP client.

This issue affects mint: from 0.1.0 before 1.9.2.
