items.summary:
Cross-site scripting vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_live_view allows an attacker to bypass URL scheme validation and execute JavaScript in a victim's browser session.

The Phoenix.LiveView.Utils.valid_destination!/2 and Phoenix.LiveView.Utils.valid_live_navigation_destination!/2 functions in lib/phoenix_live_view/utils.ex rely on an internal uri_scheme/1 helper that only detects a scheme when the input's first byte is an ASCII letter. Inputs beginning with an ASCII control character or space fall through to a nil-returning clause, causing the URL to be treated as a safe relative path.

Standard browsers implement the WHATWG URL parser, which strips leading C0 control and space characters before parsing. As a result, an input such as " javascript:alert(1)" is passed unchanged into <.link href={...}> and, when clicked, is parsed by the browser as a javascript: URL that executes attacker-controlled script in the victim's session.

Applications that render user-supplied URLs (for example profile links, redirect targets, or external references) via <.link href={...}> are affected.

This issue affects phoenix_live_view: from 1.2.2 before 1.2.7.

items.summary:
Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in elixir-mint hpax allows unauthenticated denial-of-service via unbounded HPACK integer decoding.

hpax decodes HPACK variable-length integers with no upper bound on the decoded value or the number of continuation octets. HPAX.Types.decode_remaining_integer/3 accumulates the integer as int + (value <<< m), shifting by 7 more bits for each continuation octet and stopping only on a terminating octet or truncated input, never because the integer grew too large. Because BEAM integers are arbitrary precision, a run of N continuation octets builds an O(N)-bit bignum and re-adds into an ever-larger bignum on each step, so the total decoding cost is superlinear (about O(N^2)). An unauthenticated attacker who can send an HTTP/2 header block to a server using this decoder (reached through the HPAX.decode/2 entry point) can supply a small header block that forces a large, attacker-controlled amount of CPU (and transient memory), a denial-of-service amplification.

This issue affects hpax: from 0.1.0 before 1.0.4.

items.summary:
SQL Injection vulnerability in elixir-ecto postgrex allows an attacker who can influence a LISTEN channel name to inject SQL into the reconnect replay query, causing a denial of service of the notification connection.

Postgrex.Notifications sanitizes channel names with quote_channel/1, which doubles double quotes so the name is safe inside a double-quoted identifier. This protects the single-statement LISTEN and UNLISTEN paths. On every (re)connect, however, handle_connect/1 replays all registered channels at once by concatenating their LISTEN statements and wrapping them in a dollar-quoted anonymous code block (DO $$BEGIN ... END$$). quote_channel/1 does not escape the $$ dollar-quote delimiter that opens and closes this block.

The listen/3 guards only reject null bytes and names longer than 63 bytes, so a channel name containing $$ passes validation unchanged. Once such a name is embedded, its $$ prematurely terminates the outer dollar-quoted string and PostgreSQL parses the remainder as additional top-level statements. Because handle_connect/1 runs on every (re)connect, the malformed replay query is rejected each time and the notification connection never re-establishes its subscriptions, silently dropping notifications for every channel sharing that connection.

An application is affected when it passes untrusted input (for example a tenant or user identifier) as a channel name to Postgrex.Notifications.listen/3. The double-quote doubling prevents forming a fully valid injected statement, so arbitrary SQL execution is not possible, but the corrupted query reliably breaks the shared notification connection for all tenants, resulting in denial of service.

This issue affects postgrex: from 0.16.0 before 0.22.3.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Podman. This issue may allow an attacker to create a specially crafted container that, when configured to share the same IPC with at least one other container, can create a large number of IPC resources in /dev/shm. The malicious container will continue to exhaust resources until it is out-of-memory (OOM) killed. While the malicious container's cgroup will be removed, the IPC resources it created are not. Those resources are tied to the IPC namespace that will not be removed until all containers using it are stopped, and one non-malicious container is holding the namespace open. The malicious container is restarted, either automatically or by attacker control, repeating the process and increasing the amount of memory consumed. With a container configured to restart always, such as `podman run --restart=always`, this can result in a memory-based denial of service of the system.

While certain services operate within the confines of limited PCP user/group privileges, others are granted full root privileges. This disparity in privilege levels poses a risk when privileged root processes interact with directories or directory trees owned by unprivileged PCP users. Specifically, this vulnerability may lead to the compromise of PCP user isolation and facilitate local PCP-to-root exploits, particularly through symlink attacks. These vulnerabilities underscore the importance of maintaining robust privilege separation mechanisms within PCP to mitigate the potential for unauthorized privilege escalation.

The issue occurs because the parser uses a single internal variable to store both the remaining chunk size and state flags. This can allow a second, "smuggled" request to be processed out of sync, potentially bypassing security controls.

items.summary: The Organize Media Folder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'EXIF.DateTimeOriginal' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.00 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. This bypass of wp_filter_post_kses means the injected payload survives regardless of the uploader's unfiltered_html capability; Subscriber-level access becomes sufficient when a front-end attachment-upload integration such as bbPress with forumAttachments is active, and exploitation requires no special configuration because the %created_timestamp% placeholder is included in the caption template by default. Exploitation by attackers with subscriber-level access and above requires that bbPress and gd-bbpress-attachments (forumAttachments) are installed and configured so that Subscribers/Participants can post attachments through a frontend forum form. On a default installation, where that is not configured, the vulnerability requires attackers with author-level access and above.

This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to include arbitrary PHP files that reside within the active theme's root directory (bounded because '/' inside an attribute value terminates parse_url()'s host and is then percent-encoded and stripped), and — when the shipped-default 'Unsafe features' option remains on — to read arbitrary post meta of any post, on any front-end page that renders [su_qrcode data="%CURRENT_URL%"].

items.summary: A flaw was found in gst-plugins-base. A heap buffer overflow can be triggered when processing video buffers whose attached GstVideoMeta metadata declares plane strides and offsets that exceed the actual backing memory allocation. The metadata is not range-checked during deserialization, and the video frame mapping code does not verify that the declared plane geometry fits within the buffer before allowing consumers to read or write video data. A local attacker who controls the sending side of a GStreamer inter-process IPC pipeline can deliver a crafted buffer carrying fabricated strides, causing the receiving process to read or write beyond heap boundaries. Successful exploitation can cause a denial of service or potentially allow code execution within the affected process.

items.summary: @fastify/rate-limit is the rate-limiting plugin for the Fastify web framework. Starting in version 11.1.0, the plugin documented a manual flow for limiting failed login attempts that peeks at the limiter, runs the password check, and consumes a slot only on failure. Because the peek and the consume are two separate store operations with the password check in between, concurrent requests can all pass the peek before any slot is consumed, so in versions 11.1.0 through 11.2.2 a burst of requests runs far more failed attempts than the configured limit, and the sequential path also allowed one attempt more than configured. The default per-request limiter is not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/rate-limit 11.3.0, which makes the manual flow atomic by reserving a slot in a single operation and refunding it only on success, and users should upgrade to 11.3.0 or later.

items.summary:
Uncaught Exception vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix allows an unauthenticated attacker to cause a denial of service via a client-selected legacy serializer on binary channel broadcasts.

When an application broadcasts {:binary, data} payloads on a channel topic, any client that connects without a vsn parameter, or with vsn=1.0.0, and joins that topic makes those broadcasts fail. Phoenix.Channel.Server.send/4 encodes each broadcast with every subscriber's own serializer inside the PubSub dispatch loop, calling fastlane!/1 with no rescue, and the negotiated Phoenix.Socket.V1.JSONSerializer raises Protocol.UndefinedError on a binary payload. Every binary broadcast on the topic then crashes the broadcasting process and skips every subscriber dispatched after the attacker. For broadcasts arriving from other nodes the loop runs in the PubSub adapter worker, whose repeated crashes restart the PubSub supervisor and empty the node's subscription registry while sockets stay connected.

This issue affects phoenix: from 1.5.7 before 1.5.16, from 1.6.0-rc.0 before 1.6.18, from 1.7.0-rc.0 before 1.7.25, and from 1.8.0-rc.0 before 1.8.17.

Improper Input Validation vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix (Phoenix.Presence) allows an attacker who can join a channel to cause a denial of service via a non-string presence key.

track/3,4 accepts any term as the presence key, such as a JSON object taken from a join payload. The shard then terminates, taking down every channel and LiveView process tracked on it and erasing presence state for all its topics. Repeated joins exhaust the restart intensity and take down the application supervisor.

This issue affects phoenix: from 1.2.0 before 1.5.16, from 1.6.0-rc.0 before 1.6.18, from 1.7.0-rc.0 before 1.7.25, and from 1.8.0-rc.0 before 1.8.17.

items.summary:
The AIL Framework web application contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in its dashboard templates. In the home dashboard (dashboard.html), the hunter trackers dashboard (trackers_dashboard.html), and the objects dashboard (objs_dashboard.html), object global identifiers (GIDs) derived from filenames or message IDs were interpolated directly into inline JavaScript event handler attributes (onmouseenter/onmouseleave) within HTML anchor tags. Because the GID value was placed inside a single-quoted JavaScript string literal within an HTML attribute, an attacker who could control the GID value (for example, by crafting a filename or message ID containing a single quote) could break out of the string context and inject arbitrary JavaScript code that would execute in the context of any user viewing the dashboard.

Additionally, in dynamically generated JavaScript code within the same templates, object identifiers were concatenated into HTML strings and inline event handler registrations without sufficient encoding, presenting a similar injection surface. The AJAX tooltip lookup also concatenated the raw GID into a URL without encoding, which could be leveraged for further manipulation.

The vulnerability requires that an attacker be able to influence the GID value stored in the application (e.g., through a file upload or message creation with a crafted name) and that a victim subsequently visits one of the affected dashboard pages and hovers over the affected object link. Successful exploitation allows execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session, potentially leading to session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

items.summary:
The STM32 SMBus driver (drivers/smbus/smbus_stm32.c) implements smbus_block_read() and smbus_block_pcall() by issuing a single i2c_transfer() in which the byte-count byte returned by the peripheral is read directly into the len field of the following i2c_msg. That message then receives data straight into the caller-supplied buffer. Nothing bounds the count, so smbus_stm32_block_read() and smbus_stm32_block_pcall() read up to 255 bytes into a buffer that the SMBus API documents (and the syscall verifiers validate) as holding at most SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX (32) bytes.

The count is chosen by the addressed SMBus peripheral. A malicious, counterfeit or faulty device on the bus (for example a removable smart battery, PMBus supply or plug-in module), or anyone able to drive the bus lines, can report a block count above 32 and cause the driver to write up to 223 bytes past the end of the caller's buffer. Callers typically pass a 32-byte stack buffer, as the in-tree smbus block_read shell command does, so the overflow lands on the caller's stack before any caller-side count check can run.

The result is attacker-controlled stack or memory corruption in the context of the calling thread, which can crash the system or potentially be leveraged for code execution. When the call arrives through the smbus_block_read/smbus_block_pcall system calls, the out-of-bounds write happens in supervisor mode beyond the 32-byte region validated for the user thread. The fix receives the block into a driver-local 255-byte buffer and copies it out only when the count is at most SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX, returning -ENODATA otherwise.

items.summary:
The system call verification handlers for smbus_block_read() and smbus_block_pcall() in drivers/smbus/smbus_handlers.c (z_vrfy_smbus_block_read() and z_vrfy_smbus_block_pcall()) validated the device object, the count pointers and (for process call) the send buffer, but never validated the receive buffer (buf / rcv_buf). The call then proceeds into the driver implementation, which runs in supervisor mode and writes the bytes received from the SMBus peripheral through that pointer.

A user-mode thread on a system built with CONFIG_USERSPACE that has been granted access to an SMBus device object can pass an arbitrary address, including kernel data or another thread's memory, as the receive buffer. The driver then writes up to SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX (32) bytes of peripheral-supplied data there (the STM32 driver writes as many bytes as the peripheral's length byte announces, up to 255). The address is fully attacker-chosen; the written content comes from the bus and is typically influenceable by the caller through the choice of peripheral and command, or by first writing data to a device that echoes it back.

This breaks the user/kernel isolation boundary: it gives an unprivileged thread a kernel-memory write primitive usable for privilege escalation, or at minimum to corrupt kernel state or crash the system. The fix adds K_SYSCALL_MEMORY_WRITE() checks of the receive buffer for the documented worst case, SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX. Systems without CONFIG_USERSPACE are not affected.

items.summary:
Observable Discrepancy vulnerability in Drupal CAPTCHA for Drupal 7 allows unauthenticated attackers to test login credentials despite CAPTCHA protection.

When CAPTCHA is enabled on Drupal login forms, normal form validation can still run after a missing or incorrect CAPTCHA response. This may expose credential validation feedback and allow an attacker to distinguish invalid credentials from valid credentials paired with a failed CAPTCHA.



This issue affects CAPTCHA for Drupal 7: from 7.x-1.0 through 7.x-1.7.

items.summary:
ethernet_send() in subsys/net/l2/ethernet/ethernet.c dropped the caller's reference on an IPv4 packet whenever net_arp_prepare() returned NET_ARP_PKT_REPLACED. That return value is also used when ARP could not queue the packet because every ARP cache entry is already pending. In that case ARP holds no reference of its own, so the original packet was freed before the replacing ARP request was transmitted.

If transmitting the ARP request then failed (a driver send error or an ethernet_fill_header() failure), the error path called net_pkt_ref() on the freed packet. net_if_tx() then called net_pkt_unref() on it again. If the freed net_pkt slab slot was reallocated in between, the stray unref releases a reference owned by an unrelated packet, which is freed while still in use.

An attacker on the local link can drive the ARP cache into the all-pending state. CONFIG_NET_ARP_TABLE_SIZE defaults to 2, so it is enough to elicit replies to a few spoofed, non-responding on-subnet addresses. Reaching the memory corruption also needs a transmit failure the attacker does not directly control and a narrow slab-reuse race. The practical impact is corruption or a crash of the network stack (denial of service).

items.summary:
usbh_req_setup() in subsys/usb/host/usbh_ch9.c returns -ETIMEDOUT as soon as a control request times out, even though the transfer is still in flight. usbh_xfer_dequeue() only requests cancellation, and the host controller driver keeps the transfer and its data buffer until it returns it through the completion callback. Callers such as usbh_req_desc_dev() and usbh_req_desc_cfg() free the buffer (net_buf_unref()) right after usbh_req_setup() returns. Separately, a single global semaphore (ch9_req_sync) with no mutual exclusion lets a late or foreign completion wake the wrong waiter. That waiter then returns early and its caller frees a buffer the controller is still filling.

A malicious USB device attached to a Zephyr USB host port can trigger this during enumeration. It NAKs a GET_DESCRIPTOR request until the 5-second timeout expires, then answers with data around the cancellation, or delays its answer to the next request after leaving a stale semaphore signal. The controller driver (for example the MAX3421E max3421e_hrslt_success() path) then writes device-controlled bytes into the freed net_buf and updates its length.

The result is a use-after-free write into the USB host buffer pool with attacker-chosen contents, which can corrupt buffers that have been reallocated to other transfers, plus a leak of transfer objects. Crashes or memory corruption follow. The fix serializes usbh_req_setup() with a mutex, resets the semaphore before each request, and waits for the driver to return a cancelled transfer before freeing it. Only builds with the experimental CONFIG_USB_HOST_STACK are affected.

items.summary:
The Zephyr TFTP client in subsys/net/lib/tftp/tftp_client.c does not check where the reply to its request comes from. After sending a read or write request to the configured server, send_request() accepts the first UDP datagram that arrives on the client's socket from any address and port. It then calls zsock_connect() to that sender, so the sender becomes the peer for the rest of the transfer. RFC 1350 requires a client to discard datagrams whose source does not match the transfer ID it expects.

A host that can send a UDP datagram to the client's ephemeral port before the real server replies can take over the transfer. It can reply from its own address and does not need to spoof the server. A host on the same network segment that sees the request can do this easily. An off-path attacker must guess the randomized ephemeral port and win the race, which is easier when the server is slow or unreachable. No authentication or user interaction is needed beyond the device starting a transfer through tftp_get() or tftp_put(), for example from an application or the net tftp shell command.

For tftp_get(), the attacker chooses the entire content handed to the application's data callback. For tftp_put(), the whole upload buffer is sent to the attacker. There is no memory corruption. TFTP itself has no authentication, and after the fix an attacker who can spoof the server's IP address can still interfere with a transfer. The fix checks the server's address on the first reply and the full address and port on every later datagram, and drops mismatches without using up the transfer's retries.

items.summary:
The Intel SoC FPGA Agilex5 SoC's static MMU region table in soc/intel/intel_socfpga/agilex5/mmu_regions.c mapped the System Manager peripheral (sysmgr) with MT_P_RW_U_RW. That sets the EL0 access-permission bit in the page-table descriptor, so user mode can read and write the block. The other peripheral windows in the same table, and the same block on the sibling Agilex SoC, are correctly mapped MT_P_RW_U_NA.

On arm64, memory-domain page tables are cloned from the kernel page tables (arch_mem_domain_init()). When CONFIG_USERSPACE is enabled, every user mode thread therefore gets direct load/store access to the System Manager registers, with no partition grant or system call. Any untrusted code running as a user thread can exploit this.

The System Manager controls system-wide state that only the kernel should own: NoC/FPGA-bridge idle requests, SDMMC and EMAC interface configuration, FPGA interface enables and boot scratch registers. A user thread can stall the interconnect or reconfigure peripherals out from under kernel drivers, causing denial of service and integrity loss for the platform, and can read that configuration. This breaks the userspace isolation boundary. Builds without CONFIG_USERSPACE (the default) are not affected. The fix maps the region MT_P_RW_U_NA.

items.summary:
The mount-time recovery scan of the Zephyr Memory Storage (ZMS) key-value store, zms_recover_last_ate() in subsys/kvss/zms/zms.c (subsys/fs/zms/zms.c in older releases), computes the end of the sector's data area incorrectly. Every valid allocation table entry (ATE) reset the data-end bound to the start of the sector, including entries whose value is stored inline (8 bytes or less) and delete entries. When the newest ATE in the active sector is one of these, the scan continues past the ATE area into the payload area and reads stored value bytes as struct zms_ate records.

Any payload slot that passes the ATE check (a CRC8 plus the one-byte sector cycle count) is adopted as the newest entry. zms_init() then sets fs->ate_wra and fs->data_wra from it. The pointers are only this weak check away from data an application may have stored on behalf of a remote party: a BLE-writable device name, provisioned credentials, or configuration received over the network. An attacker who can get about 16 bytes of chosen content persisted in a ZMS value can plant a forged ATE. The forged entry takes effect after the next mount, provided the newest entry in that sector is small or a delete. Random data can also match by chance, which is how the issue was found.

A forged or accidentally matched ATE overrides the stored entry for any chosen id. Its inline data or its offset/len pointer controls what later reads of that key return. The misplaced write pointers also make later writes place ATEs and payloads over other entries' existing data, silently corrupting persistent configuration such as settings values stored in ZMS. The effects are limited to the active flash sector and to what ZMS returns to its callers. No RAM out-of-bounds access was identified.

items.summary:
The Intel SEDI I2C controller driver (drivers/i2c/i2c_sedi.c, used on Intel ISH platforms) waits for each asynchronous transfer with k_sem_take() on a per-controller completion semaphore and a 1 s timeout. When the wait times out, i2c_sedi_api_full_io() aborts the transfer via SEDI_I2C_ABORT_TRANSFER, but if the controller's completion interrupt fires between the timeout expiring and the abort masking interrupts, the callback k_sem_give()s the semaphore and the token is never discarded.

The next transfer on that bus then takes the stale token immediately and returns success (the stale context->err is usually 0) while the controller is still executing it. The HAL interrupt handler (or DMA) keeps copying received bytes into the caller's msgs[i].buf. Since I2C callers typically pass stack buffers, this writes into a stack frame that has already been returned from, and the caller also consumes incomplete data. The desynchronization can persist across later transfers.

Triggering the race requires a transfer to complete just after the 1 s timeout. A device on the I2C bus that controls clock stretching (for example a malicious or tampered peripheral) can steer this timing, and it also supplies the bytes that get written. Exploitation therefore needs physical access to the bus and is timing-dependent. The impact is corruption of kernel or thread stack memory with data the peripheral controls, which can lead to a crash or potentially to code execution. The fix calls k_sem_reset() and clears context->err after the abort, while the transfer mutex is still held.

items.summary:
Several Bluetooth LE Audio services in subsys/bluetooth/audio register global connection and authentication callbacks but assume every connection is LE. When CONFIG_BT_CLASSIC is enabled, the host also invokes these callbacks for BR/EDR connections. For such connections bt_conn_get_dst() returns NULL, and bt_conn_get_info() leaves info.le.dst unset (zero or uninitialized stack data). The CSIP Set Member (csip_disconnected(), handle_csip_disconnect(), handle_csip_auth_complete()), PACS (pacs_auth_pairing_complete(), pacs_security_changed()) and HAS (security_changed(), client_alloc(), client_free()) callbacks then compare or copy a Bluetooth address through that NULL or uninitialized pointer.

A remote device within Bluetooth range can trigger this against a dual-mode device that exposes LE Audio server roles and accepts BR/EDR connections. Opening and closing a BR/EDR ACL link, with no pairing, reaches the CSIP Set Member disconnect path. Completing SSP pairing (for example Just Works) or encryption reaches the PACS and HAS paths.

The impact is denial of service. With CONFIG_ASSERT enabled, the device halts on an assertion (bt_keys_find_addr(), context_alloc()). On platforms that trap NULL or wild reads, it crashes. Otherwise, internal PACS/CSIP/HAS client state is corrupted with bogus addresses. The defects are reads only, and the attacker does not control the address that is dereferenced. The fix adds bt_conn_is_type(conn, BT_CONN_TYPE_LE) checks at the top of the affected callbacks.

items.summary: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.46.0, social account linking can use an unverified email returned by the standard OAuth 2.0 or Azure AD connector to select an existing local account. When findSocialRelatedUser matches a victim's email and a request to POST /api/experience/identification enables linkSocialIdentity, an attacker who controls that unverified provider email can link an attacker-controlled social identity to the victim account and sign in as the victim. The issue applies when the provider does not verify email ownership or allows the value to be set freely; Google, GitHub, and default OIDC connector behavior is not affected because those paths expose only verified email. Version 1.46.0 adds an opt-in email synchronization control to the standard OAuth 2.0 connector, while the Azure AD connector has offered an equivalent opt-in control since version 1.43.0. These controls preserve existing behavior by default, so administrators must enable them on affected connectors. A configurable mitigation is available in version 1.46.0.

An unauthenticated client can send a non-WRITE DSIFUNC_CMD packet with a nonzero dsi_code smaller than dsi_len, causing dsi_stream_receive to consume only the dsi_code number of payload bytes and leave attacker-controlled bytes in the readahead buffer. The residual bytes become the next DSI header, allowing protocol desynchronization that can close sessions, corrupt protocol state, or trigger an infinite-read denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 4.4.3.

items.summary: The WP Import Export Lite plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Limited Code Injection in all versions up to, and including, 3.9.32 via the 'comment' parameter. This is due to a two-stage shortcode check that evaluates the raw mapping placeholder before data substitution, causing the neutralizer to be skipped when attacker-controlled comment content containing a malicious [wpie_function] shortcode is substituted at runtime. This can lead to session theft, account hijacking, and further attacks against site users.

This issue affects Icon API 7.1.0.

items.summary: Budibase is an open-source low-code platform. Prior to 3.50.0, the public POST /api/global/users/init endpoint on a self-hosted single-tenant deployment accepts an attacker-controlled tenantId and evaluates checkAnyUserExists() in the selected tenant database instead of the legitimate default tenant. An unauthenticated attacker can select an unused tenant namespace to bypass the one-time initialization guard, causing packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts to create a tenant-specific CouchDB database and a global-administrator document without a session or CSRF token. Repeating this operation with unique tenant identifiers can exhaust datastore resources and leave latent privileged records. The created administrator cannot log into the default tenant while multi-tenancy remains disabled, which limits the immediate impact to persistent writes, denial of service, and records that may become usable during later multi-tenant operation or migration. This issue is fixed in versions 3.50.0 and 4.0.0.

items.summary: In EDB Postgres Extended Server and EDB Postgres Advanced Server versions 15 through 18 with Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) enabled, the key used to encrypt temporary files was incompletely initialized. The code applied sizeof() to a pointer to the key buffer rather than to the buffer itself, so only 8 of the intended 32 bytes were filled from a secure random source and the remaining 24 bytes kept whatever was already in memory. This reduces the guaranteed randomness of the temporary-file key from 256 bits to 64 bits. Exploiting this requires local read access to the server's temporary-file directory, and those files normally exist only while the server is running; they persist only after a crash and are removed at the next server start. Permanent data files and WAL are not affected. The issue is fixed in EDB Postgres Extended Server 15.20, 16.16, 17.12 and 18.7 and EDB Postgres Advanced Server 15.20.0, 16.16.0, 17.12.0 and 18.7.0; the server must be restarted after upgrading.

items.summary:
When NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source is configured to use TLS 1.3 early data using the ssl_early_data on directive, an attacker can use a specially crafted TLS 1.3 connection to drive an NGINX worker into a tight loop in which it repeatedly retries the same send without ever making progress. The worker continues accepting new connections and handling existing ones, but one CPU core is pinned at 100%.

Impact:
System performance can degrade until the NGINX worker process is either forced to restart or is manually restarted. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a degradation of service that can lead to a denial-of-service (DoS) on the NGINX system. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.

Note: Software versions which have reached End of Technical Support (EoTS) are not evaluated.

items.summary: Psono Server Community Edition versions 1.12.6 through 7.5.0 and Psono Server Enterprise Edition before 7.5.1 do not require accepted group membership when authorizing deletion of group share-rights. The DELETE /share/right/ endpoint checks for a membership matching the target group, the authenticated user, and share_admin=True, but omits accepted=True. An authenticated remote attacker who has been invited to a group with share-admin privileges, and who knows a group share-right UUID, can therefore delete that group's share-right record without accepting the invitation or after declining it. Pending invitations have accepted=None, while declined invitations retain accepted=False and the share_admin flag. Deletion revokes the group's access to the affected share and its contained secrets for all accepted group members, without deleting the underlying data or disclosing secret contents. The issue was fixed in version 7.5.1 of both editions, released on 2026-10-13.

items.summary:
Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character encoding, in the GNU C Library version 2.3.3 and later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.

When converting from UCS-4, these encoders may encounter a combining base such as U+00E6 and jump ahead by 4 bytes to check the next UCS-4 code point.  The check for end of buffer however does not account for this, which may result in a buffer overread if the following code point has less than 4 bytes remaining.  Exploitation of this bug not only requires attacker control of input and encoding, but also strict control over layout of the input in memory.

items.summary:
A privilege escalation flaw was found in the scan_mysql actor of leapp-upgrade-el9toel10 (provided by leapp-repository). During RHEL 9 to RHEL 10 upgrades, the actor runs:
mysqld --validate-config --log-error-verbosity=2 directly as root in the Leapp actor context, bypassing the packaged MySQL systemd unit that normally starts the daemon as User=mysql.

A process compromised as the mysql OS identity can write a version-2 persisted configuration (mysqld-auto.cnf) and a malicious shared object into /var/lib/mysql (a directory owned by mysql). That persisted map can set plugin_dir to /var/lib/mysql and early_plugin_load (or related loader options such as plugin_load / plugin_load_add) so MySQL loads the attacker-controlled object during configuration validation. Plugin loading can reach dlopen() before MySQL’s runtime-user check and before plugin-symbol validation.

When an administrator subsequently runs the documented Leapp preupgrade or upgrade workflow, attacker-controlled code can execute as UID 0 with a full capability set in an unconfined SELinux domain (unconfined_t). The attack does not require write access to the default system plugin path under /usr; redirecting plugin_dir via mysql-owned persisted state is sufficient. Ordinary SQL privileges alone (including highly privileged SQL accounts) are not a sufficient startpoint — OS-level execution as the mysql service identity is required, plus later administrator invocation of Leapp.

items.summary:
MISP contains a DOM-based cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the Pivot Explorer component. The bundled pivotick visualization library (version 1.2.0) rendered all string values it received as HTML markup rather than as plain text. As a result, user-controllable data fields, including attribute comments, attribute values, and reference relationship types, were interpreted and executed as HTML/JavaScript in the Pivot Explorer tooltip and sidebar panels.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify MISP attributes could embed malicious HTML or script payloads in these fields. When another user (or the same user) opened the Pivot Explorer and viewed the affected event data, the injected markup would execute in the victim's browser context, potentially allowing session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must have authenticated access to create or modify MISP attributes (comments, values, or reference relationship types).
- The victim must open the Pivot Explorer and interact with or view the affected event data in the tooltip or sidebar.

Security impact: Successful exploitation allows arbitrary script execution in the victim's browser within the MISP application origin, enabling theft of session credentials, manipulation of displayed data, and execution of privileged API calls on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP's brute-force lockout mechanism for login and one-time-password (OTP) authentication is susceptible to bypass through Unicode case-folding inconsistencies and input handling flaws.

- Email addresses containing non-ASCII capital letters are not counted toward the lockout threshold, permitting unlimited authentication attempts against a specific account.
- Database collation folding (accent and width variants) allows an attacker to reach a valid account using a folded alias of the email address without the attempt being recorded in the lockout counter.
- A password containing a NUL byte produces a distinct server error for known accounts while unknown accounts receive a different response, enabling username enumeration.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit these issues to perform unlimited password brute-force attacks against any account and to enumerate valid user accounts.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52

items.summary:
MISP contains multiple flaws in its login and one-time-password (OTP) brute-force lockout mechanism that collectively weaken authentication protection.

- Lockout counter bypass: the lockout stored and matched usernames using a single-byte case-fold function. An email address containing a non-ASCII capital letter (for example a Latin-1 or Cyrillic uppercase) was never counted toward the lockout threshold, allowing unlimited failed login attempts against that account.
- Collation-folding authentication bypass: the database collation performs accent and width folding, so a Unicode variant of a valid address (e.g. a different diacritic or a full-width character) resolved to the same account during authentication while the lockout treated it as a distinct, untracked identity. An attacker could therefore authenticate as the target user using a folded alias without triggering the lockout.
- Username enumeration via NUL byte: submitting a password containing a NUL byte caused the hashing routine to raise an exception, producing an HTTP 500 response for a known account but a different response for an unknown one, disclosing valid usernames.

Preconditions: the target MISP instance is reachable over the network and the login endpoint is exposed. No prior authentication is required.

Security impact: an unauthenticated attacker can perform unlimited password-guessing against accounts whose address contains a non-ASCII capital, can authenticate as a user via a Unicode-folded alias, and can enumerate valid usernames. Successful exploitation leads to account takeover.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP contains a type confusion vulnerability in the authentication key creation endpoint. When a user submits a floating-point value as the target user identifier, the authorization check truncates the value to an integer (matching the attacker's own account), while the persistence layer rounds the same value to a different integer (the next account in the sequence). This discrepancy allows an authenticated user with key-creation permission to generate an API authentication key belonging to another user.

Preconditions:
- The attacker must be an authenticated user with the permission to create authentication keys.
- The target user must have a consecutive numeric identifier immediately following the attacker's identifier.

Impact:
- Unauthorized creation of an API key for another user, granting the attacker access to that user's data and operations within the MISP instance.
- The vulnerability is trivially exploitable by substituting a carefully crafted floating-point value for the integer user identifier in the request.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP contains multiple related authorization and input-validation flaws in its object editing and attachment handling workflows.

- A user with permission to edit their own object could inject a foreign attribute identifier into the object revision form. The revision data, stored in the server-side session, was merged into the stored object before the save diff was computed. The save then wrote to the foreign attribute row by its identifier without verifying that the row belonged to the caller's event or organisation, allowing an attacker to overwrite or soft-delete an attribute in another organisation's private event.
- Attachment file paths were constructed directly from event and attribute identifiers supplied by the request. Because no type or format validation was applied, crafted values (for example directory-traversal sequences or file-name extensions) could cause the application to read from or write to file-system locations outside the intended attachment directory.
- The audit-log behaviour recorded an edit under the event identifier carried in the save payload rather than the event identifier of the stored database row. An attacker who included a different event identifier in the save could cause the audit entry to be attributed to the wrong event, undermining the integrity of the audit trail.

Exploitation requires an authenticated web-session user with object-editing permissions (perm_add / perm_modify). API-key-only requests do not carry the PHP session and are not affected by the revision-session vector.

Affected versions: MISP < 2.5.52. Fixed in 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP contains an improper output sanitization vulnerability in the Zeek (Bro) intelligence export functionality.

The export module constructs tab-separated lines for downstream Zeek/Bro intelligence feeds. The sanitization routine was intended to strip tab, newline, and carriage-return characters from user-controlled fields (organisation names and attribute values) before they were embedded into the export line format. However, the sanitization pipeline applied character replacement before HTML entity decoding, meaning that HTML entities such as 	 (tab), 
 (newline), and  (carriage return) survived the initial pass and were subsequently decoded into actual separator characters. Additionally, organisation names were inserted into the export format string without any sanitization at all.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify events, organisation names, or attribute values could embed HTML-encoded separator characters. When the Zeek/Bro export was generated, these characters would split a single export line into multiple lines or introduce extra tab-delimited fields, corrupting the structured intelligence feed consumed by downstream Zeek/Bro deployments.

Security impact:
- Integrity of exported intelligence data is compromised; downstream Zeek/Bro systems may process malformed or split entries.
- Corrupted intelligence lines could lead to incorrect blocking, alerting, or logging decisions in the consuming environment.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP contains a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) vulnerability in its Warninglist feature. Warninglist entries of type "regex" are evaluated against attribute values without any backtracking limit. An authenticated user with permission to add or import warninglist entries can supply a crafted regular expression pattern that triggers excessive backtracking in the PCRE engine, causing sustained CPU consumption and denial of service.

Additionally, imported warninglists were not validated for syntactic correctness before replacing existing entries, allowing malformed or malicious patterns to be persisted and later evaluated without prior rejection.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated account with the ability to create, edit, or import warninglist entries (users below site-admin level can add entries).
- The target MISP instance has at least one warninglist of type "regex" that will be evaluated against incoming attribute values.

Impact:
- Sustained CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service for all users of the MISP instance.
- Potential for cascading performance degradation on shared infrastructure.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP's NIDS rule export functionality for Snort and Suricata formats does not properly escape user-controlled data before embedding it into generated rule text. Attribute values, tag names, and URL paths are inserted directly into rule options (msg, metadata, content matches) without neutralizing characters that are syntactically significant in the NIDS rule grammar, such as double quotes, semicolons, backslashes, commas, and control characters.

An authenticated user with the ability to create or modify attributes in a MISP instance can craft attribute values or tag names containing these special characters. When the NIDS rules are exported, the unescaped data breaks out of the intended option or content field, allowing injection of arbitrary rule options, corruption of rule structure, or generation of syntactically invalid rules that may cause the downstream NIDS engine to reject the entire ruleset.

The affected export paths include:
- Snort and Suricata msg: option (quotes, semicolons, backslashes, control characters)
- Suricata metadata: option (commas, semicolons, quotes, whitespace, control characters)
- Suricata http.uri content: match for URL path (quotes, semicolons, pipe characters)

Security impact is limited to the integrity and availability of the exported NIDS rules and the downstream NIDS engine that consumes them. There is no direct compromise of the MISP application itself.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP contains a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in its feed and sync HTTP request handling. When the application uses libcurl as the HTTP transport, the CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION option was enabled by default, causing the library to automatically follow HTTP redirects without the application's own per-hop validation logic being invoked.

- Feed requests: MISP implements its own redirect validation for feed sources, but libcurl was following redirects before that validation could execute, allowing a malicious or compromised feed source to redirect the request to arbitrary internal URLs.
- Sync requests: Sync peers are server-configured, and the application does not perform per-hop redirect validation for sync traffic. libcurl's automatic redirect following allowed a malicious sync peer to redirect the request to internal network resources.

An attacker who is a configured sync peer, controls a feed source URL, or can influence DNS resolution for a configured endpoint can exploit this to cause the MISP server to issue requests to arbitrary internal services, potentially reading sensitive data or interacting with internal APIs that are not otherwise exposed.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP contains a denial-of-service vulnerability in its image processing pipeline. When generating attachment thumbnails or rendering event graph preview images, the application decodes user-supplied image data using the GD library without first validating the declared pixel dimensions in the image header.

Because GD allocates its pixel buffers outside the scope of PHP's memory_limit directive, a crafted image with an extremely large declared resolution (for example, 20000 x 20000 pixels) can trigger a multi-gigabyte memory allocation during the decode step, exhausting available system memory and causing the PHP worker process or the host to become unresponsive.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated MISP user with permission to upload attachments or to create/view event graphs.
- The ability to supply a crafted image file (e.g., a PNG with a valid header declaring oversized dimensions).

Impact:
- Denial of service: memory exhaustion leading to process crash or host unavailability.
- No confidentiality or integrity impact is indicated by the evidence.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

MISP contains a vulnerability in its password reset (forgot password) functionality where the base URL used to construct the reset link sent by email could be derived from the HTTP request's Host header rather than from an explicitly configured value.

An unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request with a malicious Host header. If the application's base URL was not explicitly configured (MISP.baseurl or MISP.external_baseurl), the bootstrap would derive it from the request, and the resulting password reset email would contain a link pointing to the attacker-controlled domain. When the victim clicks the link, they are directed to the attacker's site, enabling credential phishing or token theft.

Preconditions:
- The password reset feature (allow_password_forgotten) is enabled
- MISP.baseurl and MISP.external_baseurl are not explicitly set to trusted values
- The victim initiates or is targeted for a password reset

Impact:
- Phishing: victim is redirected to an attacker-controlled URL instead of the legitimate MISP instance
- Potential credential compromise if the victim enters credentials on the attacker's site
- No direct compromise of the MISP server itself

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52

- Bypass of the intended access-control model for sharing group membership

- Data (events, galaxies, clusters, analyst notes, sightings) can be created under an organisation the attacker does not belong to, polluting that organisation's data and potentially exposing it to that organisation's members.
- New organisations can be created from attacker-supplied identifiers, introducing phantom entities into the MISP instance.
- The integrity of the threat-intelligence data store is compromised because attribution is no longer trustworthy.

Affected: MISP versions prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary:
MISP's interactive CLI shell, when used to edit or disable a user account, did not update the user record's modification timestamp. The application's session validation mechanism relies on this timestamp to detect that a user's record has changed and to reload the user's state in all active sessions.

As a result, a user who was disabled or had their role or permissions modified through the CLI would retain their existing authenticated session and continue to operate with their previous privileges until the session naturally expired. The administrative intent to revoke or reduce access was not enforced on already-active sessions.

Preconditions:
- An administrator performs a user edit or disable action via the MISP interactive CLI shell rather than the web interface.
- The target user has one or more active web sessions at the time of the change.

Impact:
- A disabled user retains full access to the MISP instance for the duration of their existing session.
- A user whose role or permissions were reduced via the CLI continues to operate with their prior, higher privileges in open sessions.

Affected versions: MISP prior to 2.5.52.

items.summary: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 7.1.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, it opens the upstream WebSocket connection with a header set built by the default header rewriter, which forwards the client cookie but never sets the upstream origin option, so the browser origin header is dropped while the authenticating cookie is forwarded. Many WebSocket servers defend against cross-site hijacking by checking the origin and treat a missing origin as a trusted non-browser client, so behind the proxy that check never sees the foreign origin. A malicious page visited by a logged-in user can therefore open a WebSocket through the proxy to an upstream that authenticates the handshake with a cookie, and read or send messages on the user's behalf. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later. As a workaround, provide a header rewriter that sets a correct origin, or validate the origin before the proxy.

The underlying send step answers with a forbidden response, but the listing fallback misreads that response on a path ending in a slash as a directory without an index file and serves the listing anyway. items.summary: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.0.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, a WebSocket upgrade that is pipelined behind another HTTP request on the same cleartext connection arrives while that request's response is still attached to the socket. The shared upgrade listener sees the socket is already claimed and returns early without taking the upgrade, but it does not attach an error listener to the raw socket, and Node.js has already removed its own error listener before emitting the upgrade event. A later socket error on that connection, such as a client connection reset, is therefore unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. A single unauthenticated connection that pipelines an upgrade behind a normal request and then resets is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. Upgrades over TLS are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

items.summary: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions before 11.6.10, it rejects destinations containing parent-directory path segments by an exact string match, so a segment that carries a semicolon path parameter, such as a dot-dot segment followed by a semicolon and an optional parameter, is not equal to the plain dot-dot form and passes the check, and the WHATWG URL parser keeps it as an ordinary segment so the rewrite-prefix containment check also passes. Servlet containers such as Apache Tomcat and Jetty strip semicolon path parameters from each segment before resolving dot-segments, so a request routed through the configured prefix is rewritten and reaches the upstream where it resolves above the intended subtree, escaping the path the proxy is meant to expose and, on some containers, crossing application contexts. Both the HTTP and WebSocket proxy paths are affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

items.summary: @fastify/static is the Fastify plugin for serving static files. In versions before 10.1.8, the allowedPath guard receives only the requested pathname, but the underlying send step selects the file to serve afterwards, so a request for a directory resolves to its default index file and an extensionless request resolves through the configured extensions to a matching file. The selected file is streamed without being re-checked against allowedPath, so a guard that denies a specific file is bypassed by requesting its directory or extensionless form. An unauthenticated client can read files inside the static root that the application meant to keep private whenever the denied file is reachable as a directory index or an extension match. The issue is fixed in @fastify/static 10.1.8, and users should upgrade to 10.1.8 or later. As a workaround, also deny the directory and extensionless forms in allowedPath, or disable the index and extensions options.

items.summary:
ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick use small modules, called "coders", to read each image format. When processing images, TYPO3 determined the coder from the file type detected by the file contents, as long as the detected mime-type started with image/. A file containing MVG (Magick Vector Graphics) instructions, uploaded with an image file extension like .png, was therefore processed with the MVG coder. MVG instructions can read local files into the processed image, which allows disclosing the contents of arbitrary files readable by the web server, for example configuration files containing credentials, through a publicly accessible processed image.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires a way to upload files without a mime-type check, for example a public form of the Form Framework using a FileUpload or ImageUpload element without configured allowedMimeTypes (see TYPO3-CORE-SA-2026-032), which allows exploitation by unauthenticated visitors. Additionally, ImageMagick must be used for image processing, and its default system configuration must allow the MVG coder.

items.summary:
The installer (first installation wizard) could be re-enabled on an already configured instance by placing a file whose name starts with FIRST_INSTALL in the public web root or the project root. The installer then became accessible without authentication, allowing for example to change the database connection and to create a new administrator and system maintainer account, which leads to remote code execution. As demonstrated in TYPO3-CORE-SA-2026-026, such a file could be created by an authenticated, low-privileged backend user without any further permissions. Other ways of creating files in the web root, as well as leftover or restored marker files, could be abused in the same way.

With the fixed versions, the installer can no longer be re-enabled on an already configured instance by a marker file. A new internal setting $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['SYS']['isInstalling'] is stored in the system configuration and is only enabled while a new installation is running. Additionally, only the exact file names FIRST_INSTALL and FIRST_INSTALL.txt are accepted as marker files.

items.summary:
The Strava datasource plugin's resource handler POST /strava-api forwards a client-supplied endpoint string, and its query parameters, to the Strava API (https://www.strava.com/api/v3/<endpoint>) without validation.

When the datasource is not in OAuth pass-through mode, the request is made with the access token stored on the datasource, not the caller's identity. Grafana authorises plugin resource calls only on the datasources:query permission, which Viewers have by default. Any such caller could therefore request any Strava API path the connected account's OAuth grant allows, for example athlete/clubs or routes/{id}, and read the response.

The plugin's frontend (stravaApi.ts) only needs a fixed set of paths: athlete, athlete/activities, activities/{id}, activities/{id}/streams and segments/{id}.

Requests to Strava are GET only, so the issue is read-only.

Affected: plugin versions 1.2.0 through 1.7.2. The fix restricts endpoint to those five patterns and is pending release. The check runs before the access token is resolved, so a rejected request never causes a token refresh or any call to Strava. Paths with .. segments are rejected as well.

items.summary:
An unauthenticated stored and reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the embedded web interface of Frontier Smart Technologies Venice X FS2340 running IR4.9 allows a network attacker with access to the interface to inject attacker-controlled JavaScript that may execute in the browser of a user accessing affected content.



Successful exploitation may allow the attacker to access information available within the browser's security context or perform actions through the affected web interface with the privileges of the affected user.



During authorized security testing, certain crafted JavaScript and code-injection payloads were also observed to cause the embedded web interface to crash and become temporarily unavailable on some tested software versions. This behavior represents a denial-of-service condition affecting the embedded web management interface; no device-level denial of service was established.

items.summary: Synchronet BBS, in versions 3.20b to 3.21e, contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the answer() function when processing the terminal attribute of the SSH service. The call to cryptGetAttributeString() does not limit the copy to the size of the destination buffer, of which 41 bytes are used. An unauthenticated remote client can send a TERM value of up to 64 bytes and overwrite adjacent fields of the session object. If the SSH service is enabled, this tampering can cause connection threads to be blocked for an extended period, even after the client has disconnected. By exhausting the available sockets, the attacker can prevent new connections and cause a denial of service requiring the software to be restarted.

items.summary: When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. A third party who controls data a tool returns, such as a record that an MCP server or a function tool returns from an external system, can use this to make the application download a URL on its local network, or make the model provider read an s3:// object or uploaded file with the application's credentials. Applications are affected when tool results can contain third-party data, message history containing those results is serialized and loaded again (stored history, history a UI adapter holds on the server, or Temporal, DBOS or Prefect durable execution), and the model is one Pydantic AI downloads files for, one that honors force_download, or one whose provider resolves non-HTTP file URLs or uploaded files. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0.

When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact: validation bypass, as extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted JSON data into models allowing extra data (with extra='allow'), with a key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__ (e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=...)], int]), using Pydantic from 2.13.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.2.

Python mode validation isn't affected.

items.recommended_action: 建议根据原文自行评估
items.summary:
Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them. As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

items.summary:
### Summary ui

With `strip_ansi=True`, Pydantic AI Harness's `ToolOutputLimits` capability removes ANSI escape sequences from tool output with a pattern that takes time quadratic in the length of a line. A tool result of a few hundred kilobytes, crafted with many unterminated escape sequences, can occupy the event loop for tens of seconds to minutes, delaying every other request and agent run in the process.

### Details

This affects applications that set `strip_ansi=True` on `ToolOutputLimits` (named `OverflowingToolOutput` before 0.13.0) and run tools whose output an attacker can influence, such as shell commands, file reads, fetched pages or MCP servers. Stripping runs on the event loop before the capability reduces the output, so its own size limits do not bound it.

The assumed attacker can place text in content a tool returns.

### Mitigation

Upgrade `pydantic-ai-harness` to 0.70.0 or later. Until then, leave `strip_ansi` at its default, `False`.

On Pydantic AI v1, the harness cannot be upgraded past 0.4.0. Upgrade to Pydantic AI v2 and `pydantic-ai-harness` 0.70.0, or leave `strip_ansi` off.

items.summary:
PagePdfDocumentReader and ParagraphPdfDocumentReader are vulnerable to a denial of service when processing untrusted PDF input.



 The underlying text extraction logic reconstructs layout from a PDF's glyph positions and limits how much memory can be allocated for any single computed gap, but does not limit the cumulative allocation across an entire page.



A specially crafted PDF can exploit this to force excessive memory allocation during processing, resulting in OutOfMemoryError.



Depending on JVM configuration, this can cause request failures with degraded service under repeated exploitation, or immediate JVM termination when ExitOnOutOfMemoryError options are used.



Any application that processes PDFs from untrusted sources (document upload, email attachment processing, RAG ingestion, web crawling) using either affected reader is impacted.

items.summary:
The UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 2.26.16.26, UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 1.26.16 do not keep serialized string lengths consistent when their database search and replace processes certain serialized values, allowing users with a role as low as Subscriber to plant data that becomes an attacker-chosen PHP object after an administrator runs a URL-lengthening search and replace or a migration restore.

When the replacement changes the length of the text, the declared string lengths inside the stored value no longer match and the corrupted value is written back, so when WordPress later reads it the trailing bytes are parsed as further serialized structure, including an object of a class the attacker named. No gadget chain is known in the UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 2.26.16.26, UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 1.26.16 themselves; further impact depends on classes available from other installed code.

The UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 2.26.16.26, UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 1.26.16 do not preserve long database values byte-for-byte when restoring a database backup, allowing users with a role as low as Subscriber to plant a serialized value that becomes a PHP Object Injection once an administrator backs up and restores the database.

No gadget chain is known in the UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 2.26.16.26, UpdraftPlus: WP Backup & Migration Plugin WordPress plugin before 1.26.16 or WordPress core, so the demonstrated effect is instantiation of an attacker-chosen class in the attacker's own requests. Exploitation requires the planted data to line up exactly with how the backup is read back, which depends on details of the attacker's row and the database dump format.

the Matter and Aliro Door Lock Application of the Nordic Semiconductor nRF Door
Lock and Access Control Add-on v1.0.0 through v1.1.1 with
CONFIG_DOOR_LOCK_STEP_UP_PHASE enabled, deleting a Credential Issuer passes the
1-based Matter credential index to ClearValidityIterations(), which expects a
0-based storage index. The intended issuer's ValidityIteration state is left in
place, and the state of the adjacent, still-provisioned issuer is cleared. This
resets that issuer's rollback protection. An attacker holding an older but correctly
signed Access Document from the adjacent issuer, whose validity iteration had
been superseded, can then potentially obtain physical access. Fixed in v1.2.0.

items.summary:
In the Aliro access control reference
  applications of the Nordic Semiconductor nRF Door Lock and Access Control
  Add-on v1.0.0 through v1.1.1, built with Credential Issuer CA
  certificate-based issuer trust (CONFIG_DOOR_LOCK_CREDENTIAL_ISSUER_CA) and
  the Aliro Step-up phase (CONFIG_DOOR_LOCK_STEP_UP_PHASE) enabled,
  AccessManagerImpl::ProcessValidityIteration() treats a failed lookup of the
  Credential Issuer in the provisioned issuer array as success. For an issuer
  trusted through a certificate chain but not provisioned, the
  ValidityIteration (credential-rollback) check is therefore skipped. A former
  authorized holder with an old but correctly issuer-signed Access Document can
  be granted physical access after the issuer has advanced its iteration to
  revoke that credential. The default Matter provisioning configuration is not
  affected. Fixed in v1.2.0.

items.summary:
A flaw was found in the interaction between systemd-gpt-auto-generator and 
confidential computing guest VM images in OpenShift Sandboxed Containers 
(confidential peer pods). systemd-gpt-auto-generator automatically discovers 
and mounts GPT partitions by type GUID at boot with no user confirmation. In 
the confidential computing threat model, where the host/hypervisor is the 
adversary, a malicious host can inject partitions into the guest's virtual 
disk. Most critically, injecting a swap partition causes the guest kernel to 
page out TEE-encrypted memory to a host-controlled block device, breaking the 
confidentiality guarantee of the hardware TEE (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX).

The PodVM images use a GPT-partitioned disk with dm-verity on the root 
partition. However, the roothash= kernel parameter only disables root 
auto-discovery — non-root partitions (swap, /home, /var, /srv, /var/tmp) are 
still auto-discovered and mounted. The generator is shipped unmasked in the 
RHEL systemd-udev subpackage, and no kernel command line parameter in the 
measured UKI addon disables it. Additionally, the PodVM measurement script 
captures PCRs 3, 9, 11, and 12, but not PCR 5 (GPT partition table), so 
partition table modifications are not detected by remote attestation.

An explicit role "name" taken from a role's meta/requirements.yml is used to construct the on-disk installation path without validating that the resulting destination stays within the selected roles directory. A name containing "../" escapes that directory, and an absolute name replaces it entirely. Because ansible-galaxy processes transitive dependencies from an installed role's meta/requirements.yml, a malicious role publisher can cause attacker-supplied files to be written outside the operator's chosen roles directory when the operator installs the role, and, when --force is used, can cause an existing role directory outside that path to be removed and replaced. The impact is bounded by the invoking user's filesystem permissions and requires the operator to install the attacker-influenced content.

Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime vulnerability in elixir-grpc grpc_server allows a client to stall all later calls on a shared HTTP/2 connection via calls that the server refuses while their DATA frames are in flight.

The stream handler grpc_stream_h (grpc_server/src/grpc_stream_h.erl) requests flow from Cowboy only for request data that has arrived. This issue affects grpc_server: from 1.0.0 before 1.1.0.

The part delimiter, the header separator, and the line endings cost nothing.

In lib/plug/parsers/multipart.ex, Plug.Parsers.MULTIPART.parse_multipart_headers/5 keeps an entry for every part without a content-disposition header, together with its header list, until the whole body is read. Any endpoint that uses Plug.Parsers with the :multipart parser is reachable.

This issue affects plug: from 1.13.0 before 1.20.4.

This could alter the timeline shown to analysts and cause configured data retention strategies to delete affected records earlier than intended.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API accepts client-supplied values for timestamps that Splunk SOAR uses to order records and apply data retention.
The early deletion impact requires an applicable data retention strategy; the timeline impact does not.
For more information see Manage your PostgreSQL database with data retention strategies (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/6.4.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-system-health-and-performance/manage-your-postgresql-database-with-data-retention-strategies) in the Splunk documentation.

When another user views the imported note, Splunk SOAR could run unauthorized JavaScript in the browser of that user, exposing data and allowing actions available to that user.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not sanitize HTML note content during container import before it renders the content in Mission Control.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the Assets edit or delete permission and access to one or more tenants could change or delete assets assigned to other tenants through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. With this access, the user could redirect connector traffic and expose the credentials and operational data associated with an asset, or disrupt integrations and data ingestion for other tenants.

items.recommended_action: 建议根据原文自行评估
items.summary:
A bug related to the Zookeeper HTTP endpoints in Apache Solr allows an authenticated attacker with zk-read permission to read /security.json, bypassing the security-read authorization check. This may cause unauthorized read of credential hashes and authorization configuration.

For this attack to be successful, the following must be true
  *  The system is secured with Solr's Basic Auth plugin
  *  The attacker has gained direct network access to the Solr cluster
  *  The attacker has obtained credentials for a user account with zk-read permission (which is recommended assigned to trusted admins only)

items.summary:
A vulnerability was found in FreeIPA in a way when a Kerberos TGS-REQ is encrypted using the client’s session key. This key is different for each new session, which protects it from brute force attacks. However, the ticket it contains is encrypted using the target principal key directly. For user principals, this key is a hash of a public per-principal randomly-generated salt and the user’s password.

If a principal is compromised it means the attacker would be able to retrieve tickets encrypted to any principal, all of them being encrypted by their own key directly. By taking these tickets and salts offline, the attacker could run brute force attacks to find character strings able to decrypt tickets when combined to a principal salt (i.e. find the principal’s password).

A vulnerability was found in FreeIPA in how the initial implementation of MS-SFU by MIT Kerberos was missing a condition for granting the "forwardable" flag on S4U2Self tickets. Fixing this mistake required adding a special case for the check_allowed_to_delegate() function: If the target service argument is NULL, then it means the KDC is probing for general constrained delegation rules and not checking a specific S4U2Proxy request.

In FreeIPA 4.11.0, the behavior of ipadb_match_acl() was modified to match the changes from upstream MIT Kerberos 1.20. However, a mistake resulting in this mechanism applies in cases where the target service argument is set AND where it is unset. This results in S4U2Proxy requests being accepted regardless of whether or not there is a matching service delegation rule.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Jolokia's JSR-160 proxy functionality where insufficient validation of client-controlled JMX service URLs allows a bypass of the denylist introduced to mitigate CVE-2018-1000130. The proxy accepts a `target.url` value from a Jolokia POST request and passes it to `JMXServiceURL` and `JMXConnectorFactory` for establishing the remote JMX connection. The existing denylist only rejects URLs matching `service:jmx:rmi:///jndi/ldap:.*`, which can be bypassed using alternative valid JMX service URL forms, including `ldaps://` schemes or LDAP URLs with a non-empty JMX host component. These URLs are accepted as valid `JMXServiceURL` objects and can cause the Jolokia agent JVM to perform a JNDI lookup against an attacker-controlled LDAP endpoint. This can result in server-side request forgery (SSRF), forwarding of supplied JMX credentials to the remote endpoint, and potentially remote code execution depending on the classes and configuration available in the target JVM.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/sqpoll: don't wait for the thread to exit

io_sq_thread_stop() wakes the SQPOLL thread and waits for it to exit.
The thread belongs to the thread group that created the ring, so a
SIGSTOP or the cgroup freezer holds it in get_signal(), and the wake up
doesn't change that. io_ring_exit_work() then sleeps in that wait until
someone continues or kills the process. iou_exit has 64 slots, so 64
closed SQPOLL rings of a stopped process keep every other ring from
being freed, for everyone.

Don't wait. Set the stop bit, wake the thread, and let it exit when it
gets to run again. The sqd can now outlive its last ring, so give it a
second refcount with one reference for the rings and one for the thread,
and free it with the last one. The thread can't reach a freed ring,
rings leave ctx_list before dropping their reference, and the io-wq hash
is refcounted.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/cancel: drop sqd->lock while SQPOLL waits

An exiting SQPOLL thread calls io_uring_cancel_generic() with sqd->lock
held, and keeps it across cond_resched() and the sleep until nothing is
in flight anymore. A zero-copy send notification can't be canceled and
stays pending as long as the peer doesn't read, so the lock is held for
as long as a user cares to. io_ring_exit_work() needs it to park the
thread, and so do IORING_REGISTER_IOWQ_AFF and IOWQ_MAX_WORKERS. With
64 such rings sharing the thread, every iou_exit slot sleeps on the lock
and no ring gets freed for anyone.

Drop the lock around cond_resched() and the sleep, like the main loop of
the thread does. Each walk of ctx_list is still under one hold, and
nothing is kept across the unlock. The thread drops its io-wq, frees its
tctx and clears sqd->thread under one hold after the loop, so whoever
holds the lock and finds sqd->thread set can still use them.

[axboe: adapted to the schedule_timeout() based loop]
